questions.stem: An engineer has an existing `CiliumPodIPPool` named `default` that pods on the cluster are already using, and wants to modify that resource in place. Which modification does the excerpt say is possible?

It is required, because externalTrafficPolicy: Cluster always masquerades the source IP, so the backend Pod can never see it.
It is unnecessary, but only if the healthCheckNodePort is manually configured so that every node passes the health check.

questions.explanation: The excerpt explicitly says that for Cilium's ingress config, both Ingress and Gateway API, it is not necessary to configure externalTrafficPolicy: Local to keep the source IP visible to the backend pod via the X-Forwarded-For and X-Envoy-External-Address fields. The statement that Local is the only way in kube-proxy clusters applies generally, but the excerpt says Cilium ingress config works differently.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt does mention that in clusters that use kube-proxy, Local is the only way to ensure source IP visibility, but it then says that for Cilium ingress config things work differently and Local is not necessary.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt says that with Cluster the node may masquerade the source IP and that in many cases the backend pod may not see it; it does not say this always happens or that the pod can never see it.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt says the healthCheckNodePort is automatically set by Kubernetes when externalTrafficPolicy: Local is set, and it does not make source IP visibility depend on manually configuring that port.

citations.title: ``externalTrafficPolicy`` for Loadbalancer or NodePort Services
citations.quote:
However, for Cilium's ingress config, both Ingress and Gateway API, **it is not
necessary** to configure ``externalTrafficPolicy: Local`` to keep the source IP
visible to the backend pod (via the ``X-Forwarded-For`` and ``X-Envoy-External-Address``
fields).

questions.stem: A platform team runs a shared cluster. They want the developers of one application team to be able to create Route objects in that team's own namespace, while ensuring those developers cannot modify the Gateway configuration or edit Route objects in any other namespace. Which aspect of the Gateway API's design is intended to make this kind of arrangement possible?

options.text: The Ingress API is deconstructed into several Gateway API objects, each aligned to a role-based persona, so that each persona gains only the specific access and privileges its responsibilities require.
Gateway API resources carry annotations that record which team owns them, and the implementation uses those annotations to restrict who may edit the resource.
The Gateway API promotes features to API conformance, which automatically grants each namespace owner write access to the Gateway configuration.
The Gateway API provides a centralized mechanism for HTTP routing, TLS termination and traffic splitting, and this centralisation removes the need for per-namespace permissions.

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that the Gateway API is designed with role-based personas in mind, in contrast to the Ingress model, which assumes a single persona where developers manage and create ingress and service resources themselves. In more complex deployments, infrastructure providers, cluster operators and application developers are all involved, and by deconstructing the Ingress API into several Gateway API objects, personas gain the specific access and privileges that their responsibilities require. The excerpt gives exactly this example: application developers in a specific team could be assigned permissions to create Route objects in a specified namespace without also gaining permissions to modify the Gateway configuration or edit Route objects in namespaces other than theirs.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt says the opposite about annotations: native support of policies for external traffic means annotations are no longer required to support ingress traffic patterns. It never describes annotations as an ownership or access-control mechanism.
optionRationale.c: API conformance is mentioned only in connection with promoting common denominators as extensions are added, to maximise the ease of extending Ingress API resources. It is not described as granting namespace owners write access to the Gateway configuration.
optionRationale.d: The centralized mechanism for HTTP routing, TLS termination, traffic splitting/weighting and header modification is a genuine feature in the excerpt, but it is not offered as the reason why per-persona permissions can be scoped; the role-based persona design is.

citations.title: Benefits of the Gateway API
citations.quote: By deconstructing the Ingress API into several Gateway API objects, personas gain the specific access and privileges that their responsibilities require.

questions.stem: An engineer creates an Ingress with an Exact path /api, an ImplementationSpecific path /api.*, a Prefix path /api, and a Prefix path /. A request for /api arrives. In the Envoy configuration that Cilium generates, which path's match is ordered first?

options.text: The Exact path /api
The ImplementationSpecific path /api.*
The Prefix path /api
The Prefix path /

questions.explanation: Cilium orders Envoy matches by path type: Exact first, then ImplementationSpecific (regular expression), then Prefix, with the / Prefix match always last. The Exact /api match therefore precedes the ImplementationSpecific /api.* and the Prefix /api matches.

optionRationale.b: ImplementationSpecific matches are ordered after Exact matches, so /api.* is not first even though it is a regex path.
optionRationale.c: Prefix matches are ordered after both Exact and ImplementationSpecific matches.
optionRationale.d: The / Prefix match has special handling and always goes last, not first.

citations.title: Ingress Path Types and Precedence
citations.quote:
#. Exact
#. ImplementationSpecific (that is, regular expression)
#. Prefix
#. The ``/`` Prefix match has special handling and always goes last.

questions.stem: You apply a `CiliumClusterwideNetworkPolicy` that denies all traffic by default, then run `curl --fail -v http://"$HTTP_INGRESS"/details/1` against the Cilium Ingress. According to the excerpt, what happens?

options.text: The request is denied: curl reports HTTP 403 Forbidden, and the Hubble flow shows the HTTP request DROPPED with a 403 response FORWARDED.
The request succeeds with HTTP 200 OK because the default-deny policy applies only to in-cluster traffic, not to external traffic arriving through the Ingress.
The request is denied with HTTP 503 Service Unavailable because Envoy cannot reach any backend once the policy is applied.
The request is dropped at the TCP layer, so curl reports a connection timeout rather than an HTTP status code.

questions.explanation: With the default-deny `CiliumClusterwideNetworkPolicy` applied, the excerpt states that the request to the `/details` endpoint is denied for external and in-cluster traffic. The curl output shows `HTTP/1.1 403 Forbidden` with `server: envoy`, and the Hubble observe output shows the `http-request DROPPED` followed by an `http-response FORWARDED` carrying the 403.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt says the request is denied for external and in-cluster traffic, so external traffic through the Ingress is not exempt.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt shows a 403 Forbidden response, not a 503 Service Unavailable.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt shows an HTTP 403 response being returned, not a TCP-level connection timeout.

citations.title: Default Deny Ingress Policy
citations.quote: With this policy applied, the request to the ``/details`` endpoint will be denied for external and in-cluster traffic.

questions.stem: A platform team has installed the standard release channel CRDs for Cilium Gateway API and now wants to use HTTPRoute Retry, which the excerpt identifies as an experimental feature in the HTTPRoute resource. What must the team do?

options.text: Install the corresponding CRDs; the experimental release channel includes everything in the standard channel plus experimental resources and fields.
Nothing further: the standard release channel already includes all experimental resources and fields.
Install the optional TCPRoute, UDPRoute and ListenerSet CRDs, because those optional CRDs enable experimental HTTPRoute fields.
Only enable the Cilium Gateway API controller with Helm or Cilium CLI; the choice of CRD release channel has no bearing on experimental features.

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that the experimental release channel includes everything in the standard release channel plus some experimental resources and fields. It gives HTTPRoute Retry in the HTTPRoute resource as an example of an experimental feature and states that, if you need such a feature, you must install the corresponding CRDs. The team therefore needs the corresponding CRDs, not merely the standard channel.

optionRationale.b: This contradicts the excerpt: the experimental channel adds experimental resources and fields beyond the standard channel.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt lists TCPRoute, UDPRoute and ListenerSet as optional CRDs for their own functionality; it does not say they enable HTTPRoute Retry.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt says to use Helm or Cilium CLI to enable the Cilium Gateway API controller once CRDs are installed, but it separately states that experimental features require the corresponding CRDs.

citations.title: Installation
citations.quote:
Note that the **experimental** release channel includes everything in the **standard**
release channel plus some experimental resources and fields. If you need
a feature that is currently marked as *experimental* (for example, HTTPRoute Retry in the ``HTTPRoute`` resource),
you must install the corresponding CRDs.

questions.stem: A team exposes a service through Cilium Ingress. A request from outside the cluster reaches the per-node Envoy and is then sent to a backend Pod with the `productpage` identity. The team is writing Network Policy and wants the request to pass both logical policy enforcement points. Which pair of allowances must the policy provide?

options.text: Allow traffic from `world` to `ingress`, and allow traffic from `ingress` to in-cluster identities such as `productpage`.
Allow traffic from `world` directly to `productpage`, and allow traffic from `ingress` to `world`.
Allow traffic only from `world` to `ingress`; the second enforcement point does not need a policy allowance.
Allow traffic only from `ingress` to `productpage`; external traffic is always assigned the `productpage` identity.

questions.explanation: Cilium Ingress has two logical policy enforcement points: one before traffic arrives at the `ingress` identity and one after, when it is about to exit the per-node Envoy. The policy must therefore allow traffic from `world` to `ingress` and from `ingress` to in-cluster identities such as `productpage`.

optionRationale.b: This reverses the required direction and skips the `ingress` identity; the excerpt requires `world` to `ingress` and `ingress` to in-cluster identities.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt says there are two logical enforcement points, so allowing only the first step is insufficient.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt says traffic from outside the cluster is usually assigned the `world` identity, not `productpage`; the second step alone is insufficient.

citations.title: Cilium's ingress config and CiliumNetworkPolicy
citations.quote:
This means that, when applying Network Policy to a cluster, it's important to
ensure that both steps are allowed, and that traffic is allowed from ``world`` to
``ingress``, and from ``ingress`` to identities in the cluster

questions.stem: You have deployed the `pod-worker` client and the `echo` server, confirmed that `pod-worker` receives HTTP `200` from `http://echo:3000/headers` while `http://echo:3000/headers-1` is denied, and verified that the SPIRE server is healthy. According to the excerpt, what must you add to enforce mutual authentication between `pod-worker` and `echo`?

options.text: Add `authentication.mode: "required"` in the ingress/egress block in your network policies.
Add `authentication.mode: "required"` to the `echo` Service definition.
Add `authentication.mode: "required"` to the `pod-worker` Pod manifest.
Add `authentication.mode: "required"` to the SPIRE server configuration.

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that, assuming the SPIRE server is healthy, adding mutual authentication simply requires adding `authentication.mode: "required"` in the ingress/egress block in your network policies. It does not say to modify the Service, the Pod manifest, or the SPIRE server configuration.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt places the setting in the ingress/egress block in your network policies, not in the `echo` Service definition.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt places the setting in the ingress/egress block in your network policies, not in the `pod-worker` Pod manifest.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt says to verify that the SPIRE server is healthy, but it places `authentication.mode: "required"` in the ingress/egress block in your network policies, not in the SPIRE server configuration.

citations.title: Mutual Authentication Example
citations.quote:
adding mutual authentication simply requires 
adding ``authentication.mode: "required"`` in the ingress/egress block in your network policies.

questions.stem: A platform team runs Cilium Gateway API behind a trusted cloud load balancer. The load balancer injects an `X-Forwarded-For` header containing the original client IP. The team wants Cilium's Layer 7 policies, including Ingress, to be applied using that client IP rather than the address of the load balancer connection. Which configuration change matches the Cilium documentation?

options.text: Set `useRemoteAddress` to `false` in the `gatewayAPI` or `ingressController` section of the values files.
Set the trusted hop count to `1` so Envoy uses the rightmost `X-Forwarded-For` value for policy decisions.
Set `useRemoteAddress` to `true` so Envoy trusts the `X-Forwarded-For` header.
Do nothing, because Envoy already uses `X-Envoy-External-Address` as the source for Layer 7 policy decisions.

questions.explanation: The excerpt says that when you trust the traffic source to inject an `X-Forwarded-For` header, you can force Envoy to treat the traffic as coming from the client IP encoded in that header by setting `useRemoteAddress` to `false` in the `gatewayAPI` or `ingressController` sections of values files. The trusted-hop count changes how Envoy derives the visible source address for `X-Forwarded-For`, and `X-Envoy-External-Address` is a header Envoy sets; neither is the documented switch for making Layer 7 policy use the `X-Forwarded-For` client IP.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt describes the trusted-hop count as controlling which `X-Forwarded-For` value Envoy uses for the visible source address, not as the documented switch for making Layer 7 policy use the client IP encoded in `X-Forwarded-For`.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt specifies setting `useRemoteAddress` to `false`, not `true`, to force Envoy to treat traffic as coming from the client IP encoded in `X-Forwarded-For`.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt says Envoy sets `X-Envoy-External-Address` to the trusted client address, but it does not say that this header is already used as the source for Layer 7 policy decisions.

citations.title: Source IP Visibility
citations.quote: ``useRemoteAddress`` to ``false`` in ``gatewayAPI`` or ``ingressController`` sections of values files.

questions.stem: A Cilium cluster has WireGuard transparent encryption enabled. Two pods that are both scheduled on the same node exchange traffic with each other, and an engineer watching the node's traffic expects to see that traffic protected by the WireGuard tunnel. What does Cilium actually do with these packets?

options.text: It leaves them unencrypted, because traffic destined to the same node it was sent from is deliberately not encrypted.
It encrypts them, because WireGuard is enabled cluster-wide for every Cilium-managed endpoint.
It encrypts them only when the two pods belong to different namespaces.
It drops them unless a CiliumNetworkPolicy explicitly allows pod-to-pod traffic on that node.

questions.explanation: WireGuard encryption in Cilium covers traffic between Cilium-managed endpoints on different nodes. When the source and the destination are the same node, the packets are not encrypted, and the excerpt states that this behaviour is intended: the raw traffic can be observed on the node anyway, so encryption would provide no benefit.

optionRationale.b: Enabling WireGuard does not encrypt every packet; the same-node case is explicitly excluded from encryption.
optionRationale.c: Namespace membership plays no part in the decision — the criterion given is whether the traffic is destined to the node it was sent from.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt says nothing about dropping same-node traffic; it says such packets are simply not encrypted.

citations.title: WireGuard Transparent Encryption
citations.quote:
Packets are not encrypted when they are destined to the same node from which
they were sent. This behavior is intended.

questions.stem: A platform team runs a Cilium cluster whose nodes are spread across several routing domains, and the routers in the underlying network have no knowledge of the cluster's PodCIDRs. According to the excerpt, what does the encapsulation model require of that underlying network?

options.text: The underlying network must be configured with the PodCIDRs so that its routers can forward pod traffic.
The topology of the underlying network is irrelevant, provided the cluster nodes can reach each other using IP/UDP.
All cluster nodes must sit within a single link-layer domain for encapsulated traffic to flow.
The PodCIDR size must be chosen to fit within the addressing limitations of the underlying network.

questions.explanation: The excerpt lists simplicity as an advantage of the model: the network connecting the cluster nodes does not need to be made aware of the PodCIDRs, and cluster nodes can spawn multiple routing or link-layer domains. The only requirement stated is reachability between nodes using IP/UDP, which makes the underlying topology irrelevant. Options a, c and d each contradict a specific statement in the excerpt.

optionRationale.a: The excerpt states the opposite: the network connecting the cluster nodes does not need to be made aware of the PodCIDRs.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt says cluster nodes can spawn multiple routing or link-layer domains, so a single link-layer domain is not required.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt says the addressing space does not depend on any underlying networking limitations, so the PodCIDR need not be fitted to them.

citations.title: Advantages of the model
citations.quote:
The topology of the underlying network is irrelevant as long as
  cluster nodes can reach each other using IP/UDP.

questions.stem: In Cilium's encapsulation model, what purpose does the excerpt give for carrying the source security identity as metadata in the network packet?

options.text: It encrypts the packet payload between the cluster nodes.
It is an optimisation designed to avoid one identity lookup on the remote node.
It lets the remote node learn the PodCIDR of the sending node.
It removes the need for cluster nodes to reach each other using IP/UDP.

questions.explanation: The excerpt explains that encapsulation protocols allow metadata to be carried along with the network packet, and that Cilium uses this to transfer metadata such as the source security identity. It then states that this identity transfer is an optimisation designed to avoid one identity lookup on the remote node. The other options describe functions the excerpt does not attribute to the identity transfer.

optionRationale.a: The excerpt describes metadata transfer for the source security identity, not encryption of the payload.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt does not link the identity transfer to PodCIDR discovery; it concerns the source security identity.
optionRationale.d: Node reachability over IP/UDP is described separately as a property of the model, not as something the identity transfer removes.

citations.title: Advantages of the model
citations.quote:
The identity transfer is an optimization
  designed to avoid one identity lookup on the remote node.

questions.stem: An operator finds that a node is reaching the default limit for authenticated relations in the Auth BPF map and wants to raise that map's upper capacity limit for cilium-agent. Which option should they use?

options.text: --bpf-auth-map-max
--bpf-map-dynamic-size-ratio
--bpf-ct-global-tcp-max
--bpf-lb-map-max

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that for some BPF maps the upper capacity limit can be overridden using command-line options for cilium-agent, and it lists --bpf-auth-map-max as the option for setting a given capacity. The Auth map has a default limit of 512k, with the scale implication of a maximum of 512k authenticated relations per node, so this is the relevant flag for raising that limit.

optionRationale.b: This flag determines the upper capacity limits of several large BPF maps at agent startup based on a ratio of total system memory; the excerpt does not list the Auth map among the maps it affects.
optionRationale.c: This flag sets a capacity for the connection tracking global TCP map, not for the Auth map.
optionRationale.d: This flag sets a capacity for the load-balancing map, not for the Auth map.

citations.title: eBPF Maps
citations.quote:
For some BPF maps, the upper capacity limit can be overridden using command
line options for ``cilium-agent``. A given capacity can be set using
``--bpf-auth-map-max``, ``--bpf-ct-global-tcp-max``, ``--bpf-ct-global-any-max``,

questions.stem: An engineer runs `kubectl get gateway -A` and sees a Gateway in the `website` namespace with class `cilium` and an address, but the `PROGRAMMED` column does not show `True`. According to the excerpt, what should the engineer check?

options.text: Make sure that Gateway API is enabled in the Cilium configuration.
Check that a LoadBalancer implementation is present.
Check that the Gateway's class is `cilium`.
Install the Gateway API CRDs.

questions.explanation: The excerpt says that if the `Programmed true` indicator is missing, you should make sure that Gateway API is enabled in the Cilium configuration. The other checks address different symptoms: a missing address points to a possible missing LoadBalancer implementation, a non-`cilium` class is not programmed by Cilium, and a missing Gateway API resource type points to missing CRDs.

optionRationale.b: This is the check suggested when no IP address appears for the Gateway, but the scenario says the Gateway has an address.
optionRationale.c: The scenario already states that the Gateway's class is `cilium`, and the excerpt says Cilium only programs Gateways with the class `cilium`.
optionRationale.d: This is the check suggested when the Gateway API resource type is not found, but the scenario has already found a Gateway resource.

citations.title: Checking resources
citations.quote: If the ``Programmed true`` indicator is missing, make sure that Gateway API is enabled in the Cilium configuration.

questions.stem: A platform team runs a global Service named rebel-base across two clusters in Cluster Mesh. In cluster 1, the Service already has service.cilium.io/global: "true". An engineer in cluster 1 runs kubectl annotate service rebel-base service.cilium.io/affinity=remote --overwrite, then runs kubectl exec -ti deployment/x-wing -- curl rebel-base from cluster 1. What should the engineer observe?

options.text: Replies from pods in cluster 2 only.
Replies from pods in cluster 1 only.
Replies from pods in both clusters as usual.
No replies, because remote affinity is only honoured when the annotation is set through a ServiceExport exportedAnnotations field.

questions.explanation: With service.cilium.io/affinity set to remote in cluster 1, the remote endpoints are preferred. The excerpt states that when cluster 1 accesses the global Service after this change, the replies come from pods in cluster 2 only. The local-only outcome belongs to the local affinity case, while the both-cluster outcome belongs to the default/no-preference case and to access from cluster 2.

optionRationale.b: This is the outcome described for affinity local, not remote: with local, cluster 1 sees replies from cluster 1 only.
optionRationale.c: This is the outcome described for the default/no-preference case and for access from cluster 2, not for remote affinity from cluster 1.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt does not say remote affinity produces no replies; it says the replies come from cluster 2 only. The MCS-API note concerns how to specify the annotation, not a condition that blocks traffic.

citations.title: Enabling Global Service Affinity
citations.quote: This time, the replies are coming from pods in ``cluster 2`` only.

questions.stem: Your cluster uses the multi-pool IPAM mode. A single CiliumPodIPPool named default currently lists 10.10.0.0/16, and running pods on two nodes hold addresses from that range. You want those workloads to receive addresses from 10.20.0.0/16 instead. According to the excerpt, what must you do?

options.text: Split the cluster into two node groups and migrate the workloads from nodes using the old CIDR over to nodes using the new CIDR.
Replace 10.10.0.0/16 with 10.20.0.0/16 in the pool and restart the existing pods so they pick up addresses from the new CIDR.
Delete the existing CiliumPodIPPool and recreate it with 10.20.0.0/16; existing pods will then be re-assigned addresses from the new CIDR automatically.
Add 10.20.0.0/16 as an additional CIDR and remove 10.10.0.0/16 in the same apply so that new pods use only the new range.

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that changing a pool's CIDR requires re-assigning the IPs of existing workloads, and that this is achieved by splitting the cluster into two node groups so workloads can migrate from nodes using the old CIDR to nodes using the new CIDR. Simply replacing the CIDR in the pool is not enough: the excerpt notes that it is not possible to delete or update CIDRs already in use, and the operator warns about CIDRs still in use by nodes.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt says it is not possible to delete or update CIDRs already in use; replacing the CIDR in the pool does not re-assign existing workload IPs.
optionRationale.c: Deleting and recreating the pool does not by itself re-assign the IPs of existing workloads; the excerpt's procedure requires node groups and workload migration.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt permits extending a pool by adding new IPv4 or IPv6 CIDRs, but it explicitly says you cannot delete or update CIDRs already in use, so removing the old CIDR in the same apply is not allowed.

citations.title: Updating existing CiliumPodIPPools
citations.quote: which allows you to migrate the workloads from nodes using the old CIDR over to nodes using the new CIDR.

questions.stem: An engineer is reviewing a CiliumNetworkPolicy that contains two ingress rules. The first rule matches a broad set of traffic, and the second matches a narrower set that overlaps with the first. A colleague is concerned that the narrower rule will somehow cut down what the broader rule permits. How does Cilium treat traffic that matches either of the two rules?

options.text: It is allowed, because the rules are additive: traffic matching the union of the rules is permitted.
It is allowed only if it matches the narrower rule, because the more specific rule takes precedence over the broader one.
It is allowed only where the two rules do not overlap, because intersecting rules cancel each other out.
It is allowed only if it matches both rules at once, because the rules in a policy are combined with a logical AND.

questions.explanation: Cilium policy rules follow a whitelist model: each rule allows the traffic that matches it, and rules are additive rather than subtractive. Where two rules overlap, the traffic matching the union of those rules is allowed, so adding a narrower rule alongside a broader one does not remove anything the broader rule already permitted. The colleague's concern is therefore unfounded. Note that traffic which matches none of the rules is dropped pursuant to the `policy_enforcement_modes`.

optionRationale.b: There is no precedence for a more specific rule in the whitelist model; a narrower rule simply adds its own matches to those of the broader rule rather than overriding it.
optionRationale.c: Rules do not cancel one another out on overlap; the excerpt states that traffic matching the union of intersecting rules is allowed.
optionRationale.d: Rules are not combined with a logical AND requiring a match against every rule; each rule independently allows the traffic that matches it.

citations.title: Rule Basics
citations.quote: If there is an intersection between two or more rules, then traffic matching the union of those rules will be allowed.

questions.stem: An engineer runs `cilium-dbg status --verbose` on a cluster where kube-proxy replacement is active. Which of the following does the verbose output report?

options.text: Mode: SNAT, with Socket LB Enabled and protocols TCP, UDP
Mode: DS NAT, with Socket LB Disabled and protocols TCP only
Mode: Hybrid, with Socket LB Enabled and protocols UDP only
Mode: SNAT, with Socket LB Disabled and protocols SCTP, TCP, UDP

questions.explanation: The verbose output in the excerpt lists `Socket LB: Enabled`, `Protocols: TCP, UDP` and `Mode: SNAT` under the KubeProxyReplacement Details.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt shows Socket LB as Enabled and protocols as TCP, UDP, and gives the mode as SNAT, not DS NAT.
optionRationale.c: The mode shown is SNAT, not Hybrid, and the protocols listed are TCP, UDP rather than UDP only.
optionRationale.d: Socket LB is shown as Enabled, not Disabled, and the protocols listed are TCP, UDP without SCTP.

citations.title: Validate the Setup
citations.quote:
Status:                True
   Socket LB:             Enabled
   Protocols:             TCP, UDP

questions.stem: You expose the `my-nginx` deployment as a NodePort service and want to confirm that Cilium's eBPF kube-proxy replacement created the service. Which command and observation match the excerpt?

options.text: Run `cilium-dbg service list` and look for NodePort entries on port 31940, one for each of devices eth0 and eth1
Run `cilium-dbg service list` and look for a single NodePort entry on port 31940 bound to eth0 only
Run `iptables-save | grep KUBE-SVC` and look for a populated KUBE-SVC rule for the service
Run `cilium-dbg status` and look for the service name `my-nginx` in the output

questions.explanation: The excerpt says that with `cilium-dbg service list` you can validate that Cilium's eBPF kube-proxy replacement created the new NodePort service, and that in the example services with port 31940 were created, one for each of devices eth0 and eth1.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt explicitly notes one service per device, for eth0 and eth1, not a single entry bound to eth0 only.
optionRationale.c: The iptables check is used to verify that no iptables rule for the service is present; the excerpt shows an empty result.
optionRationale.d: `cilium-dbg status` is used to validate the agent mode, not to list the created services.

citations.title: Validate the Setup
citations.quote:
With the help of the ``cilium-dbg service list`` command, we can validate that
Cilium's eBPF kube-proxy replacement created the new NodePort service.

questions.stem: After creating the NodePort service, an engineer runs `iptables-save | grep KUBE-SVC` in the host namespace. What result does the excerpt present as the expected confirmation?

options.text: An empty line, showing that no iptables rule for the service is present
A KUBE-SVC chain entry for each of the two backend pods
A KUBE-SVC rule for the ClusterIP only, with NodePort handled by eBPF
An error stating that iptables is not available on the host

questions.explanation: The excerpt shows the command producing an empty line and states that this verifies no iptables rule for the service is present.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt shows no KUBE-SVC entries at all, rather than one per backend pod.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt shows the output as an empty line, not a rule for the ClusterIP.
optionRationale.d: No error is shown; the output is simply an empty line.

citations.title: Validate the Setup
citations.quote:
At the same time we can verify, using ``iptables`` in the host namespace,
that no ``iptables`` rule for the service is present:

questions.stem: Which curl targets does the excerpt use to demonstrate connectivity for the exposed NodePort as well as for the ClusterIP?
questions.explanation: The excerpt shows four curl tests: the loopback address with the node port variable, the two node addresses with the node port, and the ClusterIP on port 80.

optionRationale.b: Those two addresses are the backend pod IPs shown in the service list, not the curl targets used for the connectivity test.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt uses the node port variable with 127.0.0.1 and port 80 with the ClusterIP, the reverse of this option.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt does not curl 0.0.0.0, and the ClusterIP is tested on port 80 rather than the node port.

Last but not least, a simple ``curl`` test shows connectivity for the exposed

questions.stem: A platform team has created a CiliumEnvoyConfig that produces an undesirable outcome, and they want to diagnose the problem. According to the excerpt, where should they look?

options.text: At the `CiliumEnvoyConfig` resource itself, which reports the correctness of the configuration to the user.
At the Envoy config and logs, because the CEC gives minimal feedback about the correctness of the configuration.
At the Cilium Ingress or Gateway API controller status, which validates all CECs.
At the conflict resolution report produced when multiple CECs modify the same parts of Envoy's config.

questions.explanation: The excerpt explains that `CiliumEnvoyConfig` has minimal feedback to the user about the correctness of the configuration, so when a CEC produces an undesirable outcome, troubleshooting will require inspecting the Envoy config and logs rather than looking at the `CiliumEnvoyConfig` in question.

optionRationale.a: The excerpt says the opposite: there is minimal feedback, so you cannot rely on looking at the CEC itself.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt does not describe any validation or status reporting by the Ingress or Gateway API controllers for arbitrary CECs.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt says CECs do not have a defined conflict resolution behaviour, so no such report exists.

citations.title: Caveats
citations.quote:
troubleshooting will require
  inspecting the Envoy config and logs, rather than being able to look at the
  ``CiliumEnvoyConfig`` in question.

questions.stem: Two engineers each apply a CiliumEnvoyConfig that modifies the same parts of Envoy's configuration. What does the excerpt say about the outcome?

options.text: The most recently created CEC always takes precedence.
The Cilium agent rejects the second CEC because of conflict validation.
The results may be unpredictable, because CECs have no defined conflict resolution behaviour.
The two configurations are merged deterministically, with the older CEC winning on conflicting fields.

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that `CiliumEnvoyConfig` resources have only minimal validation and do not have a defined conflict resolution behaviour, so creating multiple CECs that modify the same parts of Envoy's config may produce unpredictable results.

optionRationale.a: The excerpt describes no last-writer-wins rule; it says conflict resolution behaviour is undefined.
optionRationale.b: Only minimal validation is performed, and the excerpt does not describe rejection of conflicting CECs.
optionRationale.d: No deterministic merge rule is described; the excerpt explicitly says results may be unpredictable.

citations.title: Caveats
citations.quote:
do not have a defined conflict resolution behavior. This means that if you
  create multiple CECs that modify the same parts of Envoy's config, the results
  may be unpredictable.

questions.stem: How does the excerpt characterise `CiliumEnvoyConfig` and `CiliumClusterwideEnvoyConfig` resources with respect to access control?

options.text: They are user-facing APIs whose configuration permissions should be delegated to application teams.
They are implementation details that should be treated as cluster admin resources, with configuration permissions not delegated to other users.
They are namespace-scoped resources that any developer may edit within their own namespace.
They are read-only resources that only the Cilium Ingress controller may create.

questions.explanation: The excerpt says both resources are implementation details, should be treated as cluster admin resources, and permissions for their configuration should not be delegated to other users.

optionRationale.a: This is the opposite of the excerpt's guidance, which says permissions should not be delegated.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt does not describe namespace-scoped editing by developers; it says they should be treated as cluster admin resources.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt does not say they are read-only or that only the Ingress controller may create them — it discusses users creating CECs directly.

citations.title: Caveats
citations.quote:
are implementation details. Both should be treated as cluster admin

  other users.

questions.stem: A cluster runs Cilium's Ingress and Gateway API support, which uses `CiliumEnvoyConfig` to direct traffic through the per-node Envoy proxies. An engineer is considering creating CECs that modify the autogenerated config. What does the excerpt advise?

options.text: This is safe because Cilium's generated config is always semantically valid.
This is safe provided the CEC sets `cec.cilium.io/use-original-source-address` to `"false"`.
Be very careful, because results may be unpredictable if the CECs conflict with or modify the autogenerated config.
This is impossible, because CECs cannot be created when Ingress or Gateway API support is enabled.

questions.explanation: The excerpt warns that `CiliumEnvoyConfig` is used by Cilium's Ingress and Gateway API support, and that creating CECs which conflict with or modify the autogenerated config may produce unpredictable results, so you should be very careful using CECs for these use cases.

optionRationale.a: The excerpt says the risks are managed by ensuring Cilium-generated config is semantically valid as far as possible, not that user modifications are safe.
optionRationale.b: The annotation guidance concerns E/W traffic and source address binding, not protection against conflicts with autogenerated config.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt does not say CEC creation is blocked; it warns about the consequences.

citations.title: Caveats
citations.quote:
If you create CECs that
  conflict with or modify the autogenerated config, results may be unpredictable.
  Be very careful using CECs for these use cases.

questions.stem: According to the excerpt, what does the Cilium agent assume about the `cec.cilium.io/use-original-source-address` annotation on a CEC whose parentRefs point to the Cilium Ingress or Gateway API controllers?

options.text: That it is set to `"false"`.
That it is set to `"true"`.
That it is absent and must be supplied by the user.
That it is set to the original source address of the parent proxy.

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that the Cilium agent assumes all CECs with parentRefs pointing to the Cilium Ingress or Gateway API controllers have the annotation `cec.cilium.io/use-original-source-address` set to `"false"`, while all other CECs are assumed to have it set to `"true"`.

optionRationale.b: ``"true"`` is the assumption for all other CECs, not those with parentRefs pointing to the Ingress or Gateway API controllers.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt describes an assumption about the value, not that the annotation must be supplied by the user.
optionRationale.d: The annotation takes a string value such as ``"false"`` or ``"true"``, not an address.

citations.title: Caveats
citations.quote:
The Cilium agent assumes all CECs with parentRefs pointing to the Cilium
  Ingress or Gateway API controllers have annotation
  ``cec.cilium.io/use-original-source-address`` set to ``"false"``

kubectl annotate service rebel-base service.cilium.io/shared="false" --overwrite

questions.stem: An engineer wants to allow DNS queries for exactly three hostnames — api.example.com, db.example.com and cache.example.com — and nothing else. Which DNS policy mechanism fits, and how is it configured?

options.text: A single matchPattern entry containing all three names separated by commas.
Three separate matchName entries, one per hostname; queries matching any of them are allowed.
One matchName entry with a wildcard, such as *.example.com.
A toFQDNs rule alone, since L3 rules also permit the DNS queries themselves.

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that matchName allows queries for domains that match matchName exactly, and that multiple distinct names may be included in separate matchName entries, with queries matching any of them being allowed. A wildcard would also admit names the engineer did not list, and toFQDNs is an L3 egress rule, not the DNS query policy.

optionRationale.a: matchPattern takes a single pattern composed of literal characters and wildcards; the excerpt describes no comma-separated list of names.
optionRationale.c: A wildcard pattern would allow every subdomain of example.com, not just the three named hosts.
optionRationale.d: toFQDNs is described as an L3 egress rule selecting IPs; the excerpt does not say it permits DNS queries.

citations.title: DNS Policy and IP Discovery
citations.quote:
Allows queries for domains that match ``matchName`` exactly. Multiple
  distinct names may be included in separate ``matchName`` entries and queries
  for domains that match any ``matchName`` will be allowed.

questions.stem: An engineer writes a DNS policy with matchPattern: * intending to learn IPs for toFQDNs rules. What does the excerpt say this pattern does?

options.text: It matches all names and inserts all IPs in DNS responses into the cilium-agent DNS cache.
It matches all names but only caches IPs for names that also appear in a matchName entry.
It is rejected, because a bare wildcard is not a valid pattern.
It matches all names but caches only the first IP returned in each response.

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that a wildcard alone matches all names and inserts all IPs in DNS responses into the cilium-agent DNS cache. This is one of the convenience behaviours listed for the wildcard.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt attaches no requirement for a companion matchName entry to the bare wildcard behaviour.
optionRationale.c: The bare wildcard is explicitly described as allowed and as matching all names.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt says all IPs in DNS responses are inserted, not just the first.

citations.title: DNS Policy and IP Discovery
citations.quote:
``*`` alone matches all names, and inserts all IPs in DNS responses into
    the cilium-agent DNS cache.

questions.stem: A team is configuring Layer 7 DNS policy and is deciding which DNS traffic to intercept. What does the excerpt strongly recommend?

options.text: Intercept all DNS traffic leaving the cluster so that every resolver is covered.
Intercept DNS traffic only to the cluster DNS service, such as kube-dns.
Intercept DNS traffic only to external resolvers, leaving cluster DNS unintercepted.
Avoid interception entirely and rely on matchPattern alone.

questions.explanation: The excerpt strongly prefers intercepting DNS traffic only to the cluster DNS service such as kube-dns, because intercepting traffic to other resolvers broadens the trust boundary and may let less-trusted DNS servers influence the IPs learned for toFQDNs rules.

optionRationale.a: Intercepting all DNS traffic is the opposite of the recommendation; it broadens the trust boundary.
optionRationale.c: The recommendation names the cluster DNS service as the preferred interception target, not external resolvers.
optionRationale.d: Interception is the mechanism by which the DNS proxy collects IPs; the excerpt recommends narrowing it, not abandoning it.

citations.title: DNS Policy and IP Discovery
citations.quote:
When using Layer 7 DNS policy, strongly prefer intercepting DNS traffic
   only to the cluster DNS service, such as ``kube-dns``.

questions.stem: According to the excerpt, which DNS fields does Layer 7 DNS policy consider when allowing or disallowing traffic?

options.text: Query names or patterns of names only; other DNS fields such as query type are not considered.
Query names and query types, but not patterns of names.
Query types only, with names handled by toFQDNs rules.
All DNS header fields, including query type and response code.

questions.explanation: The excerpt says policy may be applied to DNS traffic, allowing or disallowing specific DNS query names or patterns of names, and that other DNS fields, such as query type, are not considered.

optionRationale.b: Query type is explicitly excluded, and patterns of names are explicitly supported via matchPattern.
optionRationale.c: Names and patterns are the fields considered; query type is not.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt names query type as an example of a field that is not considered, so not all header fields are used.

citations.title: DNS Policy and IP Discovery
citations.quote:
Policy may be applied to DNS traffic, allowing or disallowing specific DNS
query names or patterns of names (other DNS fields, such as query type, are not
considered).

The tests refuse to start and report a configuration error.

questions.stem: A platform team is writing a CiliumNetworkPolicy in a Cluster Mesh deployment and wants the egress rule to reach a pod named rebel-base that runs in the remote cluster called cluster2. Which label must be added to the toEndpoints matchLabels for this to work?

options.text: io.cilium.k8s.policy.cluster: cluster2
io.cilium.k8s.policy.cluster: Exists
cluster-name: cluster2
io.cilium.k8s.policy.namespace: cluster2

questions.explanation: The excerpt's first policy targets a remote endpoint by adding the label io.cilium.k8s.policy.cluster with the value cluster2 alongside the endpoint's name label. The cluster name is the one supplied through the --cluster-name agent option or the cluster-name ConfigMap option, but the label used inside the policy selector is io.cilium.k8s.policy.cluster.

optionRationale.b: Exists is used in the second policy to match any cluster, not to pin the selector to cluster2.
optionRationale.c: cluster-name is the agent option or ConfigMap option that supplies the name; it is not the label key used in the endpoint selector.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt never mentions a label key io.cilium.k8s.policy.namespace.

citations.title: Allowing Specific Communication Between Clusters

questions.stem: A team needs a policy that lets x-wing in the local cluster reach rebel-base in any cluster of the mesh, without naming each cluster individually. Which selector construction does the excerpt use for this?

matchExpressions with key io.cilium.k8s.policy.cluster and operator Exists
matchExpressions with key io.cilium.k8s.policy.cluster and operator In, listing every cluster name
A separate toEndpoints entry per remote cluster, each with its own cluster label

questions.explanation: The second policy in the excerpt allows communication to all clusters by using matchExpressions with the key io.cilium.k8s.policy.cluster and the operator Exists, which matches any endpoint carrying that label regardless of cluster.

optionRationale.a: The excerpt shows no wildcard value for the cluster label.
optionRationale.c: Listing cluster names with In would target specific clusters, not all of them, and the excerpt does not use it.
optionRationale.d: Per-cluster entries would target specific clusters rather than all clusters.

questions.stem: A cluster administrator is troubleshooting why Maglev consistent hashing is not being applied to traffic between pods on different nodes within the same cluster. According to the excerpt, which statement explains this behaviour?

options.text: Maglev hashing is applied only to external (N-S) traffic; for in-cluster service connections (E-W), sockets are assigned to service backends directly without any intermediate hop and thus are not subject to Maglev.
Maglev hashing is applied only to in-cluster (E-W) traffic; external (N-S) traffic uses random backend selection.
Maglev hashing requires XDP acceleration to be enabled for all traffic, including E-W.
Maglev hashing is disabled by default for all traffic unless maglev.hashSeed is set.

questions.explanation: The excerpt explicitly states that Maglev hashing is applied only to external (N-S) traffic and that in-cluster service connections (E-W) are not subject to Maglev because sockets are assigned to service backends directly.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt says the opposite: Maglev is for external (N-S) traffic, not in-cluster (E-W).
optionRationale.c: The excerpt mentions XDP acceleration support but does not say it is required for E-W traffic.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt does not state that Maglev is disabled by default for all traffic unless a hash seed is set; it only recommends setting the seed.

citations.title: Maglev Consistent Hashing
citations.quote:
Note that Maglev hashing is applied only to external (N-S) traffic. For
in-cluster service connections (E-W), sockets are assigned to service backends
directly, e.g. at TCP connect time, without any intermediate hop and thus are
not subject to Maglev.

questions.stem: A team is planning to change the maglev.tableSize on a running cluster. What temporary effect does the excerpt warn about?

options.text: It triggers a recalculation of the lookup table and can temporarily lead to inconsistent backend selection for new traffic until all nodes have converged and completed their agent restart.
It causes immediate packet loss for all existing connections until the table is rebuilt.
It requires a full cluster restart before any traffic can be served.
It permanently disables Maglev hashing until the hash seed is regenerated.

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that changing the table size triggers a recalculation of the lookup table and can temporarily lead to inconsistent backend selection for new traffic until all nodes have converged and completed their agent restart.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt mentions inconsistent backend selection for new traffic, not immediate packet loss for existing connections.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt refers to agent restart, not a full cluster restart.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt does not say Maglev is permanently disabled; it describes a temporary inconsistency.

citations.title: Maglev Consistent Hashing
citations.quote:
Note that changing the table
size (``M``) triggers a recalculation of the lookup table and can temporarily lead to inconsistent
backend selection for new traffic until all nodes have converged and completed their agent restart.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes a benefit of Maglev consistent hashing as presented in the excerpt?

options.text: It improves resiliency in case of failures and provides better load balancing properties because nodes added to the cluster make consistent backend selection throughout the cluster for a given 5-tuple without having to synchronize state with other nodes.
It eliminates the need for any load balancer by assigning backends at TCP connect time.
It reduces memory consumption on each Cilium-managed node compared to the random algorithm.
It guarantees that backend reassignments are exactly zero on backend removal.

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that Maglev improves resiliency in case of failures and provides better load balancing properties since nodes added to the cluster will make consistent backend selection throughout the cluster for a given 5-tuple without having to synchronize state with the other nodes.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt says in-cluster (E-W) sockets are assigned directly, but Maglev is for external traffic and does not eliminate the load balancer.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt states that enabling Maglev will have higher memory consumption compared to the default random algorithm.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt states at most 1% difference in reassignments, not exactly zero.

citations.title: Maglev Consistent Hashing
citations.quote:
This improves resiliency in case of
failures. As well, it provides better load balancing properties since Nodes added to the cluster will
make consistent backend selection throughout the cluster for a given 5-tuple without
having to synchronize state with the other Nodes.

questions.stem: An engineer is comparing Maglev with the default loadBalancer.algorithm=random. Which statement about memory consumption is correct according to the excerpt?

options.text: Enabling Maglev will have a higher memory consumption on each Cilium-managed node compared to the default of loadBalancer.algorithm=random, because random does not need the extra lookup tables.
Enabling Maglev will have a lower memory consumption because it uses a single lookup table per cluster.
Memory consumption is identical because both algorithms use the same lookup tables.
Maglev memory consumption depends only on the number of nodes, not on the table size.

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that enabling Maglev will have a higher memory consumption on each Cilium-managed node compared to the default of loadBalancer.algorithm=random given random does not need the extra lookup tables.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt says Maglev has higher memory consumption, not lower.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt says random does not need the extra lookup tables, so consumption is not identical.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt does not state that memory consumption depends only on the number of nodes; it mentions the extra lookup tables.

citations.title: Maglev Consistent Hashing
citations.quote:
Note that enabling Maglev will have a higher memory consumption on each Cilium-managed Node compared
to the default of ``loadBalancer.algorithm=random`` given ``random`` does not need the extra lookup
tables.

questions.stem: An engineer writes an egress gateway policy that lists two gateway nodes under `egressGateways`. A colleague asks whether the source endpoints matched by the policy will spread their traffic across both gateways. What is the correct answer?

options.text: Each matched endpoint egresses through a single gateway, chosen from the list, not through all of them.
Traffic is load-balanced across all gateways in the list, one connection per gateway.
Only the first entry in the list is used; the remaining entries are ignored until the first node fails.
The policy is rejected because multiple gateways require a separate policy per gateway.

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that with multiple gateways the matched source endpoints still egress through a single gateway rather than all of them, and that endpoints are assigned to a gateway based on its CiliumEndpoint's UID.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt explicitly says endpoints egress through a single gateway, not all of them, so there is no spreading of traffic across the list.
optionRationale.c: Nothing in the excerpt describes a first-entry-only or failover behaviour; assignment is based on the CiliumEndpoint's UID.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt opens by saying it is possible to select multiple gateway nodes in the same policy, so such a policy is not rejected.

citations.title: Selecting multiple gateway nodes
citations.quote:
When using multiple gateways the source endpoints matched by the policy will still egress traffic
    through a single gateway, not all of them.

questions.stem: A platform team has an egress gateway policy with several entries in `egressGateways`. They add a new node that matches one of the `nodeSelector` fields. What does the excerpt say will happen to the endpoints matched by the policy?

options.text: The list of gateways will change and the endpoints will be reassigned.
Nothing changes, because endpoint-to-gateway assignment is fixed for the lifetime of the policy.
The policy stops matching endpoints until it is reapplied manually.
All endpoints immediately move to the newly added node.

questions.explanation: The excerpt says that if a node matching one of the `nodeSelector` fields is added or removed, the list of gateways will change and the endpoints will be reassigned.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt only promises stable assignment for an endpoint's lifetime as long as the matched gateway nodes do not change; adding a matching node is such a change.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt describes reassignment of endpoints, not loss of policy matching.
optionRationale.d: Reassignment is described, but the excerpt does not say all endpoints move to the new node; assignment is based on the CiliumEndpoint's UID.

citations.title: Selecting multiple gateway nodes
citations.quote:
If a
    ``nodeSelector`` field is added, removed, or modified, or if a node matching one of the

questions.stem: How does the excerpt say endpoints are assigned to a gateway when a policy selects multiple gateway nodes?

options.text: Based on the gateway's CiliumEndpoint's UID.
Based on the order of entries in the `egressGateways` list.
Based on the source endpoint's node name.
Based on a round-robin scheme across the matched gateway nodes.

questions.explanation: The excerpt says the endpoints will be assigned to a gateway based on its CiliumEndpoint's UID.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt gives the CiliumEndpoint's UID as the basis, not the position of entries in the list.
optionRationale.c: No node-name-based assignment for the source endpoint is described in the excerpt.
optionRationale.d: Round-robin is not mentioned; the excerpt describes assignment based on the CiliumEndpoint's UID.

citations.title: Selecting multiple gateway nodes
citations.quote:
The endpoints will be assigned to a gateway based on
    its CiliumEndpoint's UID.

questions.stem: An engineer is comparing a policy with a single `egressGateway` field against one with an `egressGateways` list. Which statement about the configuration options of the list entries is correct according to the excerpt?

options.text: Entries on the `egressGateways` list have the exact same configuration options as the `egressGateway` field, and the same restrictions apply to each item.
Entries on the `egressGateways` list support a reduced set of options compared with the `egressGateway` field.
Entries on the `egressGateways` list support additional options that the `egressGateway` field does not.
The `egressGateways` list has no restrictions, unlike the `egressGateway` field.

questions.explanation: The excerpt says entries on the `egressGateways` list have the exact same configuration options as the `egressGateway` field, and that the same restrictions apply to each item of the list.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt says the options are exactly the same, not reduced.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt says the options are exactly the same, not extended.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt explicitly says the same restrictions as with the `egressGateway` field apply to each item of the list.

configuration options as the ``egressGateway`` field

questions.stem: An endpoint has been egressing through one of several gateway nodes selected by a policy. The cluster's gateway nodes matched by the `nodeSelector` fields remain unchanged. What does the excerpt say about that endpoint's gateway for the rest of its lifetime?

options.text: It should use the same gateway during its lifetime as long as the matched gateway nodes do not change.
It will be rotated to a different gateway periodically to balance load.
It will be reassigned whenever any other endpoint in the cluster is created.
It will always use the gateway with the lowest CiliumEndpoint UID in the cluster.

questions.explanation: The excerpt says an endpoint should use the same gateway during its lifetime as long as the gateway nodes matched by the `nodeSelector` fields do not change.

optionRationale.b: No periodic rotation is described; stability is tied to the matched gateway nodes not changing.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt ties reassignment to changes in the `nodeSelector` fields or the matched nodes, not to creation of other endpoints.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt refers to assignment based on the CiliumEndpoint's UID but does not describe always choosing the lowest UID in the cluster.

questions.stem: You are running Cilium 1.16 in a development cluster where no LoadBalancer Service implementation is available. You enable the Cilium Gateway API with host network mode through Helm, and a colleague asks what happened to the LoadBalancer type Service mode. What is the result?

options.text: Enabling host network mode automatically disables the LoadBalancer type Service mode, because the two are mutually exclusive.
Both modes remain active, and Cilium chooses between them per request at runtime.
Host network mode is rejected unless the LoadBalancer type Service mode is disabled first in a separate step.
The LoadBalancer type Service mode stays enabled but is limited to IPv6 listeners only.

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that enabling the Cilium Gateway API host network mode automatically disables the LoadBalancer type Service mode, and that the two are mutually exclusive. No separate manual step is required, and there is no per-request selection between the modes.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt says the modes are mutually exclusive, so they cannot both remain active with runtime selection.
optionRationale.c: The disabling happens automatically on enabling host network mode; the excerpt describes no separate prerequisite step.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt makes no such IPv6-only limitation on the LoadBalancer type Service mode; it simply says the mode is disabled.

citations.title: Host network mode
citations.quote: Enabling the Cilium Gateway API host network mode automatically disables the LoadBalancer type Service mode. They are mutually exclusive.

questions.stem: An engineer needs cross-cluster load-balancing configured directly from Cilium Service annotations, and wants granular control over how backends are shared between clusters. Which option fits, and why?

options.text: MCS-API, because it exposes Service annotations for backend sharing
Global Services, because they provide Cilium-specific cross-cluster load-balancing directly from Service annotations and allow more granular control
MCS-API, because it is the only option that supports differing Service properties per cluster
Global Services, because they replace the need for any Service annotations

questions.explanation: The excerpt describes Global Services as providing Cilium-specific cross-cluster load-balancing directly from Service annotations, and notes they are useful when you want different Service properties in each cluster or more granular control over how backends are shared.

optionRationale.a: Annotation-driven load-balancing is attributed to Global Services, not MCS-API.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt associates differing Service properties per cluster with Global Services, not MCS-API.
optionRationale.d: Global Services work directly from Service annotations, so they do not remove the need for them.

citations.title: Load-balancing & Service Discovery
citations.quote:
Global Services  provide Cilium-specific
cross-cluster load-balancing directly from Service annotations.

questions.stem: A cluster uses MCS-API and the team wants the `clusterset.local` DNS domain to work without manually editing CoreDNS configuration. According to the excerpt, what makes this possible?

options.text: CoreDNS auto-configuration, which Cilium can manage automatically when it is enabled
Global Services annotations, which inject the DNS domain
ServiceExport resources, which configure CoreDNS directly
ServiceImport resources, which replace CoreDNS entirely

optionRationale.b: Global Services are described as annotation-based load-balancing, not as the mechanism for the DNS domain.
optionRationale.c: ServiceExport is named as a resource underlying MCS-API, not as the CoreDNS configuration mechanism.
optionRationale.d: ServiceImport is named as a resource underlying MCS-API; the excerpt does not say it replaces CoreDNS.

citations.title: Load-balancing & Service Discovery
citations.quote:
which requires CoreDNS configuration
that Cilium can manage automatically when CoreDNS auto-configuration is enabled.

questions.stem: A team is deciding between the two Cluster Mesh options for cross-cluster service discovery and load-balancing. What does the excerpt say about using them?

options.text: Only MCS-API may be used; Global Services must be disabled first
Only Global Services may be used; MCS-API is mutually exclusive with it
You can use either option, or both, depending on your needs and environment
Both must always be enabled, since neither works on its own

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that Cilium supports two options for cross-cluster service discovery and load-balancing with Cluster Mesh, and that you can use either option, or both, depending on your needs and environment.

optionRationale.a: The excerpt presents MCS-API as one of two supported options, not the only permitted one.
optionRationale.b: The excerpt does not make the options mutually exclusive; it allows either or both.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt says either or both, not that both are mandatory.

citations.quote: You can use either option, or both, depending on your needs and environment.

ServiceMonitor and ServiceImport
ServiceExport and GlobalService
ServiceImport and CiliumService

questions.stem: After applying the L3/L4 policy in the demo, you run the same landing request from an xwing pod. What happens?

options.text: The request returns 'Ship landed' immediately.
The request hangs, and you must press Control-C or wait for it to time out.
The request is allowed because reply packets are always permitted.
The request is allowed because xwing pods are matched by the endpointSelector.

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that the xwing pods will be blocked, and that the request will hang, so you press Control-C to kill the curl request or wait for it to time out.

optionRationale.a: 'Ship landed' is the response for the labelled tiefighter pod, not the blocked xwing.
optionRationale.c: Stateful connection tracking applies to reply packets within an allowed connection, not to a new request from a pod the policy blocks.
optionRationale.d: The policy whitelists traffic from pods with the org=empire label; the xwing request is blocked.

questions.stem: A platform team runs Cilium's eBPF kube-proxy replacement on nodes where the native devices differ between machines, though every device name begins with the prefix eth. They want NodePort services reachable through those devices without listing each name individually. Which Helm option value should they use?

options.text: devices=eth+
nodePort.directRoutingDevice=eth+
devices='eth0,eth1,eth2'
nodePort.range="10000\,32767"

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that if the devices do not match across different nodes, the wildcard option can be used, for example devices=eth+, which matches any device starting with the prefix eth. The directRoutingDevice option concerns the single device used for direct routing between Cilium nodes, not the set of devices on which NodePort services are exposed.

optionRationale.b: The wildcard is available for directRoutingDevice too, but that option selects the direct routing device, not the devices through which NodePort services are made accessible.
optionRationale.c: This lists explicit device names, which the excerpt says must be named the same on all Cilium managed nodes — precisely the problem the team has.
optionRationale.d: This sets the NodePort port range to match a non-default kube-apiserver configuration; it has nothing to do with device selection.

citations.title: NodePort Devices, Port and Bind settings
citations.quote:
Alternatively
if the devices do not match across different nodes, the wildcard option can be
used, e.g. ``devices=eth+``, which would match any device starting with prefix
``eth``.

questions.stem: An application running in the host network namespace of a Cilium node attempts a bind(2) to a port that is used by a NodePort service. What does the application typically observe by default, and which setting opts out of this behaviour?

options.text: A bind: Operation not permitted error; setting nodePort.bindProtection to false opts out.
A bind: Operation not permitted error; setting nodePort.autoProtectPortRanges to false opts out.
The bind succeeds but traffic is silently redirected to the NodePort service; setting nodePort.range opts out.
A bind: Operation not permitted error; setting nodePort.directRoutingDevice opts out.

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that by default the NodePort implementation prevents application bind(2) requests to NodePort service ports, with the application typically seeing a bind: Operation not permitted error, and that expert users can opt out by switching nodePort.bindProtection to false.

optionRationale.b: autoProtectPortRanges controls the modification of the reserved ports list, not the prevention of bind(2) requests.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt describes the bind being prevented with an error, not succeeding with redirection.
optionRationale.d: directRoutingDevice selects the device used for direct routing; it does not govern bind protection.

citations.title: NodePort Devices, Port and Bind settings
citations.quote:
By default, the NodePort implementation prevents application ``bind(2)`` requests
to NodePort service ports. In such case, the application will typically see a
``bind: Operation not permitted`` error.

questions.stem: You have applied a CiliumClusterwideNetworkPolicy that denies all traffic by default, and you then curl the /details/1 endpoint through the Cilium Ingress from outside the cluster. What does the excerpt show happening?

options.text: The request is dropped by policy and the client receives an HTTP 403 Forbidden response served by envoy.
The request is dropped by policy and the client receives an HTTP 503 Service Unavailable response served by envoy.
The request is allowed because Cilium Ingress traffic is exempt from default deny policies, and the JSON payload is returned.
The request is dropped by policy and the connection times out with no HTTP response at all.

questions.explanation: With the default-deny CiliumClusterwideNetworkPolicy applied, the excerpt states that the request to the /details endpoint will be denied for external and in-cluster traffic, and the curl output shows an HTTP/1.1 403 Forbidden response with server: envoy. The Hubble flow confirms the http-request was DROPPED and the http-response was FORWARDED with status 403.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt shows a 403 Forbidden, not a 503 Service Unavailable; no such status appears in the source.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt explicitly says the request will be denied for external and in-cluster traffic once the default-deny policy is applied; the JSON payload only appears after ingress traffic to /details is allowed.
optionRationale.d: The curl output shows a complete HTTP response with status 403 and server: envoy, so the connection is not left to time out.

citations.quote: With this policy applied, the request to the ``/details`` endpoint will be denied for external and in-cluster traffic.

questions.stem: You are following the manual verification steps for monitoring generic IP options with Cilium. You want to inject a known Trace ID into packets sent from a client Pod to a server Pod, and you need a tool that can set IP options manually. Which approach does the tutorial take?

Deploy an nginx server and a netshoot client, then run curl from the client with a custom header carrying the Trace ID.

Deploy a netshoot server and an nginx client, then run nping from the server towards the client.

The traffic is then triggered by executing nping from the client to the server with a manually specified IP Option hex string.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt uses nping with IP options, not curl with a custom header; no header mechanism is mentioned.
optionRationale.c: The Trace ID is injected into packets with nping, not written into Pod annotations.
optionRationale.d: The roles are the other way round: nginx is the server and netshoot is the client, and nping runs from the client.

questions.stem: A colleague runs nping with the IP option string '\x88\x04\x34\x21' and asks you to confirm the payload length is acceptable. According to the excerpt, what payload lengths meet the strict length requirements?

options.text: Exactly 2, 4 or 8 bytes of payload.
Exactly 1, 2 or 4 bytes of payload.
Exactly 4, 8 or 16 bytes of payload.
Any length, provided the total option string is a multiple of four bytes.

questions.stem: In the nping example, the IP option hex string is '\x88\x04\x34\x21'. What does the excerpt say the data 0x3421 corresponds to?

Decimal 136.
Decimal 3421.
Decimal 80.

questions.stem: A cluster administrator is writing a CiliumNetworkPolicy that includes a `toPorts` entry with both an `http` rule list and a `dns` rule list for the same port. What is the outcome?

optionRationale.c: Silently dropping one member is not what the excerpt describes; mixing is disallowed outright.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt says that if none are specified no additional port level rules apply, but here two conflicting types are specified, which is a rejection case.

optionRationale.c: The excerpt describes combining or rejecting, not first-match discarding.

optionRationale.c: The opposite is true: the excerpt says traditional approaches filter on IP address and TCP/UDP ports, and that Cilium can filter on application-layer protocols such as HTTP.

questions.stem: A cluster runs Cilium in kvstore/etcd mode and the kvstore becomes unavailable. An engineer asks whether existing pods will keep having their network policy enforced. What does the excerpt say?

optionRationale.d: The excerpt describes packet drops due to policy enforcement, not rescheduling of the workload.

questions.stem: A platform team runs a cluster whose nodes are on Linux 5.15 and wants to enable BBR congestion control for Pods through Cilium's bandwidth manager. What does the excerpt say about this plan?

options.text: It will work, but only for Pods that stay in the host network namespace.
It will not work reliably, because BBR for Pods requires a v5.18.x or more recent Linux kernel.
It will work as long as eBPF Host-Routing is enabled, since the kernel version is irrelevant.
It will work, but only for Pods exposed behind Kubernetes Services.

questions.explanation: The excerpt states plainly that BBR for Pods requires a v5.18.x or more recent Linux kernel, and repeats that a 5.18 or higher kernel is needed for BBR to work reliably for Pods. A 5.15 kernel therefore does not meet the requirement, and enabling eBPF Host-Routing does not remove the kernel constraint.

optionRationale.a: The excerpt says that prior to that kernel, BBR was only working for sockets in the initial network namespace (hostns), which is the opposite of the claim that it would work for Pods there.
optionRationale.c: eBPF Host-Routing is described as an additional requirement, not a substitute for the kernel version; the excerpt explicitly ties reliability to a 5.18 or higher kernel.
optionRationale.d: Being exposed behind Services is given as the situation where BBR is particularly suitable, not as a workaround for an old kernel.

questions.stem: An engineer enables the bandwidth manager with BBR on a recent kernel but does not enable eBPF Host-Routing. According to the excerpt, what is the consequence?

options.text: The packet's socket association would be orphaned inside the host stack's forwarding/routing layer, so BBR cannot retain it until the packet hits the FQ queueing discipline on the physical device.
The kernel would stop retaining timestamps of network packets when switching from Pod to host network namespace.
Cilium would silently fall back to CUBIC for all Pods, and the status line would show EDT with BPF [CUBIC].
BBR would still work, but only for sockets in the initial network namespace.

questions.explanation: The excerpt explains that BBR needs eBPF Host-Routing in order to retain the network packet's socket association all the way until the packet hits the FQ queueing discipline on the physical device in the host namespace, and that without it the association would be orphaned inside the host stack's forwarding/routing layer.

optionRationale.b: The timestamp retention issue is attributed to older kernels, not to the absence of eBPF Host-Routing.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt does not describe any automatic fallback to CUBIC or a CUBIC status line.
optionRationale.d: Working only for sockets in the initial network namespace is what the excerpt says about kernels prior to the fix, not about missing eBPF Host-Routing.

citations.title: BBR for Pods
citations.quote: BBR also needs eBPF Host-Routing in order to retain the network packet's socket association all the way until the packet hits the FQ queueing discipline on the physical device in the host namespace.

Select BBR upon initial Cilium installation when the cluster is created, so that all nodes and Pods homogeneously use BBR.
