questions.stem: A platform team runs Cilium Cluster Mesh across three clusters. One remote cluster's connection drops and is not restored. An engineer wants Cilium to stop sending global-service traffic to that cluster's backends after a defined period, rather than continuing to use cached information. Which configuration achieves this?

options.text: Set `clustermesh.cacheTTL` to a duration greater than zero, such as `"15m"`.
Leave `clustermesh.cacheTTL` at its default of `"0s"`, which revokes caches after the built-in grace period.
Set `clustermesh.cacheTTL` to `"0s"` to force immediate revocation of cached data.
Disable global services on the unreachable cluster so its backends are removed from the cache.

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that to mitigate stale backends you can configure a cache TTL, and that to enable it you set `clustermesh.cacheTTL` to a duration greater than zero (e.g., `"15m"`). With a non-zero TTL, if the connection is lost and not re-established within that duration, Cilium revokes the cached data and stops load-balancing to the unreachable cluster's global-service backends.

optionRationale.b: The default ``"0s"`` disables the feature and means caches are never revoked, so no grace-period revocation occurs.
optionRationale.c: ``"0s"`` is the default that disables the feature; it does not force immediate revocation.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt describes configuring a cache TTL, not disabling global services on the remote cluster.

citations.title: Handling Unreachable Clusters
citations.quote: The default value is ``"0s"``, which disables this feature and means caches are never revoked.

questions.stem: How does the default value of `clustermesh.cacheTTL` affect cached service data for an unreachable remote cluster?

options.text: The default `"0s"` disables the feature, so caches are never revoked.
The default `"0s"` revokes caches immediately upon connection loss.
The default is `"15m"`, so caches are revoked after fifteen minutes.

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that the default value is `"0s"`, which disables this feature and means caches are never revoked. A duration greater than zero must be set to enable revocation.

optionRationale.b: ``"0s"`` disables the feature rather than triggering immediate revocation.
optionRationale.c: ``"15m"`` is given only as an example of a value greater than zero, not as the default.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt makes no such distinction; ``"0s"`` means caches are never revoked.

questions.stem: An engineer wants Cilium's eBPF NodePort implementation to let backends reply directly to external clients without the extra hop, and also wants policy at the backend node to be able to match on the client's source IP. Which change achieves both goals?

options.text: Set the loadBalancer.mode Helm option to dsr.
Set bpf.disableExternalIPMitigation to true.
Keep the default SNAT mode and enable the Geneve tunnel protocol.
Disable source/destination IP address checking in the public cloud provider.

questions.explanation: Setting loadBalancer.mode to dsr makes Cilium operate in DSR mode, in which backends reply directly to the external client without the extra hop and the client's source IP is preserved so policy can match on it at the backend node.

optionRationale.b: That flag disables the ExternalIP mitigation for CVE-2020-8554; it has nothing to do with DSR or source IP preservation.
optionRationale.c: SNAT mode is precisely the mode in which the client's source IP is not preserved, so keeping it cannot meet the requirement.
optionRationale.d: Disabling address checking may be necessary for DSR to work in some clouds, but it does not itself switch Cilium into DSR mode.

citations.title: Direct Server Return (DSR)

questions.stem: An operator is tuning a Cilium deployment and wants to avoid the MTU reduction that DSR would otherwise require for UDP traffic, while still using DSR for TCP. What does the excerpt say makes this possible?

options.text: For TCP services, Cilium only encodes the service IP/port for the SYN packet, not subsequent ones, which allows a hybrid mode using DSR for TCP and SNAT for UDP.
Cilium encodes the service IP/port in every TCP packet, so the MTU reduction applies equally to TCP and UDP.
The loadBalancer.mode option accepts a per-protocol value that selects DSR for TCP and SNAT for UDP.
Setting bpf.disableExternalIPMitigation to true removes the need for any MTU reduction.

questions.explanation: The excerpt notes that for TCP services Cilium only encodes the service IP/port for the SYN packet, not subsequent ones, and that this optimisation allows a hybrid mode where DSR is used for TCP and SNAT for UDP to avoid an otherwise needed MTU reduction.

optionRationale.b: This contradicts the stated optimisation, which limits encoding to the SYN packet for TCP.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt describes the hybrid mode as an optimisation arising from SYN-only encoding, not as a per-protocol value of loadBalancer.mode.
optionRationale.d: That flag relates to the ExternalIP mitigation for CVE-2020-8554, not to MTU reduction for DSR.

citations.title: Direct Server Return (DSR)
citations.quote: For TCP services, Cilium only encodes the service IP/port for the SYN packet, but not subsequent ones.

questions.stem: A team deploys Cilium in DSR mode on AWS and finds that DSR does not work. According to the excerpt, what may need to be done in such a public cloud environment?

The loadBalancer.mode must be changed back to snat because DSR is unsupported on any public cloud.
bpf.disableExternalIPMitigation must be set to true so that DSR can function.
The tunnel protocol must be switched to VXLAN, since DSR requires it in cloud environments.

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that in some public cloud provider environments that implement source/destination IP address checking (e.g. AWS), the checking has to be disabled in order for DSR mode to work.

optionRationale.c: That flag disables the ExternalIP mitigation for CVE-2020-8554 and is not presented as a requirement for DSR.
optionRationale.d: VXLAN is listed as supporting only the Geneve dispatch mode, not as a DSR requirement in clouds.

citations.title: Direct Server Return (DSR)
citations.quote: In some public cloud provider environments that implement source / destination IP address checking (e.g. AWS), the checking has to be disabled in order for the DSR mode to work.

questions.stem: An engineer enables XDP acceleration for NodePort handling and then tries to observe the packets that were pushed back out of the device for NodePort handling right at the XDP layer. Why does `tcpdump` not show them, and what should be used instead?

Packet taps come at a much later stage in the networking stack, so Cilium's monitor command or metric counters should be used instead.

questions.explanation: The excerpt notes that packets pushed back out of the device for NodePort handling right at the XDP layer are not visible in tcpdump because packet taps come at a much later stage in the networking stack, and that Cilium's monitor command or metric counters can be used instead for visibility.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt says the packets are pushed back out of the device, so they do reach it; it recommends the monitor command or metric counters, not the API server.
optionRationale.d: Disabling the acceleration is not presented as a way to gain visibility; the excerpt recommends the monitor command or metric counters.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly describes the default state of the `loadBalancer.acceleration` setting and the version in which the XDP acceleration feature was introduced?

options.text: The default is `native`, and the feature was introduced in Cilium 1.8.
The default is `best-effort`, and the feature was introduced in Cilium 1.8.
The default is `disabled`, and the feature was introduced in Cilium 1.8.
The default is `disabled`, and the feature was introduced in Cilium 1.10.

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that setting `loadBalancer.acceleration` to `native` enables the acceleration, that the option `disabled` is the default and disables it, and that the feature was introduced in Cilium version 1.8 at the XDP layer.

optionRationale.a: `native` enables the acceleration but is not the default.
optionRationale.b: `best-effort` is an option for mixed device support, not the default.
optionRationale.d: The version is wrong: the excerpt says the feature was introduced in Cilium version 1.8.

options.text: Shared Ingress ports are set globally via Helm flags, while dedicated Ingress ports are set per Ingress resource via annotations.
Shared Ingress ports are set per Ingress resource via annotations, while dedicated Ingress ports are set globally via Helm flags.
Both methods use only the ingress.cilium.io/host-listener-port annotation, differing solely in the port range.
Both methods use only Helm flags, differing solely in whether TLS passthrough is enabled.

questions.explanation: The excerpt lists two methods: Shared Ingress, configured globally via Helm flags such as sharedListenerPort, httpPort, httpsPort and tlsPassthroughPort; and Dedicated Ingress, configured per Ingress resource via annotations such as ingress.cilium.io/host-listener-port.

optionRationale.b: This reverses the two methods as described in the excerpt.
optionRationale.c: The annotation belongs to the dedicated method only; the shared method uses Helm flags.
optionRationale.d: The shared method uses Helm flags, but the dedicated method uses annotations, not flags.

citations.title: Host network mode
citations.quote: * Shared Ingress: Globally via Helm flags

questions.stem: An engineer changes ingressController.hostNetwork.sharedListenerPort from its default to a custom value. What guidance does the excerpt give about the port number to choose?

options.text: Choose a port number higher than 1023, because of binding to a privileged port.
Choose a port number lower than 1023 so that it is reserved for the ingress controller.
Choose exactly 8080, since any other value is unsupported.
Choose any port, as the excerpt gives no constraint on the value.

questions.explanation: The excerpt advises that if you change sharedListenerPort, you should choose a port number higher than 1023, referring to binding to a privileged port.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt advises a port higher than 1023, not lower.
optionRationale.c: 8080 is only the default; the excerpt explicitly contemplates changing it.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt does give a constraint: a port higher than 1023.

citations.title: Host network mode
citations.quote: If you change it, you should choose a port number higher than ``1023`` (see `Bind to privileged port`_).

questions.stem: An engineer exposes Cilium's Envoy DaemonSet through a NodePort Service in a cluster that uses kube-proxy, and the backend application must see the original client IP. Which Service setting does the excerpt say is the only way to ensure source IP visibility in this situation?

options.text: Set `externalTrafficPolicy: Local` on the Service.
Set `externalTrafficPolicy: Cluster` on the Service.
Leave `externalTrafficPolicy` unset so that Kubernetes defaults it to `Local`.
Set `externalTrafficPolicy: Local` and disable the `healthCheckNodePort`.

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that with `Local`, nodes route only to Pods on the local node without masquerading the source IP, and that in clusters using `kube-proxy` this is the only way to ensure source IP visibility.

optionRationale.b: ``Cluster`` is described as allowing the node to masquerade the source IP, so the backend pod may not see it.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt does not say that leaving the field unset defaults it to ``Local``; it only describes the two relevant settings.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt says the ``healthCheckNodePort`` is automatically set by Kubernetes when ``externalTrafficPolicy: Local`` is set, and does not suggest disabling it.

citations.title: ``externalTrafficPolicy`` for Loadbalancer or NodePort Services
citations.quote:
Because of this, in clusters that use
  ``kube-proxy``, this is the only way to ensure source IP visibility.

questions.stem: A platform team runs Cilium ingress configuration (Ingress and Gateway API) and wants the backend pod to keep the client IP visible. What does the excerpt say about the need to set `externalTrafficPolicy: Local` for this purpose?

options.text: It is required, because Cilium forwards ingress traffic to Envoy using masquerading.
It is not necessary, because Cilium always forwards ingress traffic to the local node and to Envoy via TPROXY, and the source IP remains visible via `X-Forwarded-For` and `X-Envoy-External-Address`.
It is required only for Gateway API, while Ingress works with `Cluster`.
It is not necessary, but only if the `healthCheckNodePort` is manually configured.

questions.explanation: The excerpt says that for Cilium's ingress config, both Ingress and Gateway API, it is not necessary to configure `externalTrafficPolicy: Local` to keep the source IP visible to the backend pod via the `X-Forwarded-For` and `X-Envoy-External-Address` fields.

optionRationale.a: The excerpt says ingress traffic is forwarded to Envoy using TPROXY, which transparently forwards packets, not masquerading.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt treats Ingress and Gateway API together and does not distinguish them on this point.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt does not make source IP visibility conditional on manually configuring the ``healthCheckNodePort``.

citations.title: ``externalTrafficPolicy`` for Loadbalancer or NodePort Services
citations.quote:
However, for Cilium's ingress config, both Ingress and Gateway API, **it is not
necessary** to configure ``externalTrafficPolicy: Local`` to keep the source IP
visible to the backend pod

questions.stem: A cluster uses the `multi-pool` IPAM mode. Its `default` `CiliumPodIPPool` currently contains `10.10.0.0/16`, and running pods still hold addresses from that range. The platform team must change the pool to use `10.20.0.0/16`. According to the excerpt, what approach should they use?

options.text: Split the cluster into two node groups and migrate workloads from nodes using the old CIDR to nodes using the new CIDR.
Delete the `CiliumPodIPPool` and immediately recreate it with `10.20.0.0/16`; existing pods will keep working without further action.
Add `10.20.0.0/16` as an additional CIDR and leave `10.10.0.0/16` in place; no workload migration is needed.
Update the in-use CIDR in place and restart only the Cilium operator; pods will receive new addresses on their next restart.

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that changing the CIDR of a pool requires re-assigning the IPs of existing workloads. It recommends achieving this by splitting the cluster into two node groups so that workloads can be migrated from nodes using the old CIDR over to nodes using the new CIDR. The restriction described prevents pods from receiving IPs from a new range while some pods still use the old IP pool on the same nodes, so simply recreating or updating the pool in place is not the described approach.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt does not say that deleting and recreating the pool lets existing pods keep working without further action; it describes a migration process because existing workloads must be re-assigned IPs.
optionRationale.c: Extending a pool with new CIDRs is possible, but the objective here is to change the existing default pool CIDR, and the excerpt says the restriction prevents pods from receiving IPs from a new range while some pods still use the old IP pool on the same nodes.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt does not describe updating an in-use CIDR in place as sufficient; it says it is not possible to delete or update the CIDRs already in use and gives a node-group migration procedure instead.

citations.title: Updating existing CiliumPodIPPools
citations.quote:
To change the CIDR of a pool, you need to re-assign the IPs of existing workloads. To achieve this, you can split the cluster
into two node groups, which allows you to migrate the workloads from nodes using the old CIDR over to nodes using the new CIDR.

questions.stem: An engineer maintains an existing `CiliumPodIPPools` resource that is already in use by pods. They want to add a new IPv6 CIDR to the pool. Which statement reflects the limitation described in the excerpt?

options.text: They may extend the pool by adding new IPv4 or IPv6 CIDRs, but they cannot delete or update CIDRs already in use.
They may delete an in-use CIDR once the pods using it have been cordoned, because cordoning releases the CIDR from the pool.
They may update an in-use CIDR in place, provided the Cilium operator is restarted first.
They cannot add any new CIDRs to an existing pool; a new `CiliumPodIPPools` resource must always be created.

questions.explanation: The excerpt says it is possible to extend the pool by adding new IPv4 or IPv6 CIDRs, but it is not possible to delete or update the CIDRs already in use. It also explains that this restriction prevents pods from receiving IPs from a new range while some pods still use the old IP pool on the same nodes.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt does not say that cordoning releases an in-use CIDR from the pool; it says it is not possible to delete or update the CIDRs already in use.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt does not permit updating an in-use CIDR in place after restarting the Cilium operator; it says it is not possible to delete or update the CIDRs already in use.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt explicitly says it is possible to extend the pool by adding new IPv4 or IPv6 CIDRs, so it is not true that no new CIDRs can be added to an existing pool.

citations.title: Updating existing CiliumPodIPPools
citations.quote:
It is possible to extend the pool adding new IPv4 or IPv6 CIDRs, but it is not possible to
delete or update the CIDRs already in use.

questions.stem: Cilium is running with IPsec encryption enabled. While reviewing the Cilium log files, an engineer finds a `level=warning` message reading `Device eth0 does not exist`. What does the excerpt say to do?

options.text: Set the encryption interface with `--set encryption.ipsec.interface=ethX`.
Increase the delay before old key cleanup with the agent flag `ipsec-key-rotation-duration`.
Perform a new key rotation, properly, so that the SPI is incremented.
Confirm that the IPsec `Secret` and Cilium are deployed in the same namespace together.

questions.explanation: The excerpt instructs you to check for `level=warning` and `level=error` messages in the Cilium log files, and states that if there is a warning message similar to `Device eth0 does not exist`, you should use `--set encryption.ipsec.interface=ethX` to set the encryption interface. The other options are remedies drawn from unrelated parts of the excerpt: key rotation timing, SPI handling for `XfrmInStateProtoError`, and the namespace check for Pods that fail to start.

optionRationale.b: The ``ipsec-key-rotation-duration`` flag is suggested for lengthening the delay before cleanup when key rotation is expected to take longer, not for a missing device warning.
optionRationale.c: A proper new key rotation is the fix given for ``XfrmInStateProtoError`` caused by a key update without an incremented SPI, a different symptom entirely.
optionRationale.d: The namespace check applies when the ``cilium`` Pods fail to start after enabling encryption; here the Pods are running and logging a warning.

citations.title: Troubleshooting
citations.quote:
If there is a warning message similar to ``Device eth0 does not exist``,
     use ``--set encryption.ipsec.interface=ethX`` to set the encryption
     interface.

questions.stem: A Cluster Mesh deployment spanning several clusters is rotating its IPsec keys. Because every cluster must be updated, the rotation takes considerably longer than usual, and `XfrmInNoStates` errors start appearing. Which action does the excerpt recommend?

options.text: Increase the delay before cleanup with the agent flag `ipsec-key-rotation-duration`.
Perform a new key rotation, properly, so that the SPI is incremented.
Take no action, because `XfrmInNoStates` counters are only expected to rise while a rebooted node's new key is being deployed.
Set the encryption interface with `--set encryption.ipsec.interface=ethX`.

questions.explanation: The excerpt explains that if the old key is cleaned up before the new key's configuration is installed on all nodes, `XfrmInNoStates` errors result, and that the old key is removed after a default interval of 5 minutes while agents normally update their configuration within 1 minute. Where the rotation is expected to take longer — the excerpt's own example being Cluster Mesh with several clusters to update — it recommends increasing the delay before cleanup with the agent flag `ipsec-key-rotation-duration`.

optionRationale.b: A proper new key rotation is the stated fix for ``XfrmInStateProtoError`` arising from a key update without an incremented SPI, not for slow Cluster Mesh rotation.
optionRationale.c: Rising ``XfrmInNoStates`` counters during a node reboot are indeed expected, but the excerpt separately attributes ``XfrmInNoStates`` to premature cleanup of the old key after a rotation, which is the situation described here.
optionRationale.d: The encryption interface setting addresses a ``Device eth0 does not exist`` warning and has no bearing on key rotation timing.

citations.title: Troubleshooting
citations.quote:
If you expect
   the key rotation to take longer for some reason (for example, in the case of
   Cluster Mesh where several clusters need to be updated), you can increase the
   delay before cleanup with agent flag ``ipsec-key-rotation-duration``.

questions.stem: An engineer has just added service.cilium.io/shared="false" to the rebel-base Service in cluster 1. Before removing the annotation, they run kubectl exec -ti deployment/x-wing -- curl rebel-base from cluster 1. What should they observe?

options.text: Replies from pods in both clusters.
Replies only from pods in cluster 1.
Replies only from pods in cluster 2.
No replies from any pods.

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that, after the annotation is added in cluster 1, accessing the global service from cluster 1 still shows replies from pods in both clusters.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt says that from cluster 1 the replies still come from both clusters, not only from cluster 1.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt says that from cluster 1 the replies still come from both clusters, not only from cluster 2.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt says that replies are still seen from pods in both clusters, not that no pods reply.

citations.title: Deploying a Simple Example Service
citations.quote: You will still see replies from pods in both clusters.

questions.stem: A platform engineer is writing a CiliumNetworkPolicy under the behaviour described in the excerpt. The egress rule uses toEndpoints with matchLabels name: rebel-base and does not include any cluster label or cluster match expression. Which endpoints will the policy select?

options.text: Endpoints named rebel-base in the local cluster only.
Endpoints named rebel-base in every cluster in the Cluster Mesh.
Endpoints named rebel-base in cluster2 only.
No endpoints, because a cluster label is mandatory for toEndpoints.

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that policies automatically select endpoints from the local cluster only unless one or more clusters are specifically targeted. Therefore, a toEndpoints selector with only name: rebel-base selects local endpoints. The excerpt also notes that in Cilium v1.18 or lower, policies used to select endpoints from all clusters by default, but that is not the behaviour described for the current policy default.

optionRationale.b: Selecting endpoints from all clusters was the default in Cilium v1.18 or lower, not the behaviour described for the current policy default.
optionRationale.c: Targeting cluster2 only requires an explicit cluster label such as io.cilium.k8s.policy.cluster: cluster2.
optionRationale.d: A cluster label is not mandatory; without one, the policy selects endpoints from the local cluster only.

citations.title: Allowing Specific Communication Between Clusters
citations.quote:
Policies automatically select endpoints from the local cluster only, unless one
or multiple cluster are specifically targeted.

questions.stem: A policy contains two `toPorts` entries. Both entries use the same `PortProtocol` and select an overlapping list of endpoints. The first entry defines HTTP layer 7 rules, while the second defines DNS layer 7 rules. What happens?

options.text: The policy is rejected because the layer 7 rule types differ.
The HTTP and DNS rules are combined and both are enforced.
The HTTP rules are kept and the DNS rules are silently ignored.
The DNS rules are kept and the HTTP rules are silently ignored.

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that layer 7 rules from multiple `toPorts` entries with the same `PortProtocol` and overlapping endpoints are combined only when they are of the same type. If the type differs, the policy is rejected.

optionRationale.b: Combining is permitted only when the layer 7 rules are of the same type; here the types differ.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt does not describe silently ignoring one type; a type difference causes rejection.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt does not describe silently ignoring one type; a type difference causes rejection.

citations.title: Layer 7 Policies
citations.quote: If multiple ``toPorts`` rules with identical ``PortProtocol`` select an overlapping list of endpoints, then the layer 7 rules are combined together if they are of the same type. If the type differs, the policy is rejected.

questions.stem: A policy contains a layer 4 rule for a set of endpoints and also a similar layer 4 rule with layer 7 rules for the same endpoints. What is the effect of the layer 7 portion of the second rule?

options.text: It has no effect.
It is enforced in addition to the first layer 4 rule.
It overrides the first layer 4 rule and permits only matching layer 7 requests.
It causes the policy to be rejected because layer 4 and layer 7 rules cannot coexist.

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that when a layer 4 rule is specified and a similar layer 4 rule with layer 7 rules is also specified, the layer 7 portions of the latter rule have no effect.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt says the layer 7 portions have no effect, not that they are enforced in addition.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt does not describe the layer 7 portion overriding the first layer 4 rule.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt does not say the policy is rejected; it says the layer 7 portions have no effect.

citations.title: Layer 7 Policies
citations.quote: If a layer 4 rule is specified in the policy, and a similar layer 4 rule with layer 7 rules is also specified, then the layer 7 portions of the latter rule will have no effect.

questions.stem: A CiliumNetworkPolicy has been applied that whitelists traffic sent from any pods with label org=empire to deathstar pods with label org=empire, class=deathstar on TCP port 80. A tiefighter pod carrying the label org=empire sends a POST request to deathstar.default.svc.cluster.local/v1/request-landing. What is the expected result?

options.text: The request succeeds and returns Ship landed.
The request is blocked because the policy matches endpoint IP addresses rather than pod labels.
The request hangs because Cilium connection tracking permits only reply packets, not the initial request.
The request succeeds only if the xwing pod is also labelled org=empire.

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that the policy whitelists traffic from pods with label org=empire to deathstar pods with label org=empire, class=deathstar on TCP port 80. It then says that only the tiefighter pods with the label org=empire will succeed, while the xwing pods will be blocked. Therefore the tiefighter request succeeds and returns Ship landed.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt states that endpoint IP addresses are irrelevant when defining security policies; matching is by pod labels.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt describes stateful connection tracking as automatically allowing required reply packets; it does not say the initial request is blocked.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt says xwing pods will be blocked; the tiefighter request succeeds because the source pod has org=empire, not because xwing is labelled.

citations.title: Apply an L3/L4 Policy
citations.quote: Now if we run the landing requests again, only the *tiefighter* pods with the label ``org=empire`` will succeed. The *xwing* pods will be blocked!

questions.stem: An engineer is writing a CiliumNetworkPolicy for pods that may be rescheduled to different nodes. They are deciding whether to select the pods by endpoint IP address or by pod label. What does the excerpt say they should do?

options.text: Use endpoint IP addresses, because they remain stable when pods are rescheduled.
Use the labels assigned to the pods, because endpoint IP addresses are irrelevant and policies are applied based on labels irrespective of where or when the pod is running.
Use the deathstar service DNS name, because Cilium policies match on service names rather than pod identity.
Use both endpoint IP addresses and pod labels, because Cilium requires an IP address in every policy rule.

questions.explanation: The excerpt says that endpoint IP addresses are irrelevant when defining security policies and that labels assigned to pods should be used instead. It adds that policies are applied to the right pods based on labels irrespective of where or when the pod is running within the cluster.

optionRationale.a: The excerpt says endpoint IP addresses are irrelevant when defining security policies, not stable selection keys.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt discusses pod labels and endpoint IP addresses; it does not say policies match on service DNS names.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt says to use labels instead of endpoint IP addresses; it does not require both.

citations.title: Apply an L3/L4 Policy
citations.quote: When using Cilium, endpoint IP addresses are irrelevant when defining security policies. Instead, you can use the labels assigned to the pods to define security policies.

questions.stem: A platform team has installed Cilium with the host firewall enabled and applied a CiliumClusterwideNetworkPolicy that uses a NodeSelector to select a group of worker nodes. On one of those selected nodes, two workloads send traffic to destinations outside the cluster: pod A runs with hostNetwork: true, while pod B runs in its own pod network namespace. How does the host policy treat these two flows?

options.text: Both flows are covered, because the policy selects the node on which both pods are running.
Pod A's traffic is covered, because host policies apply to the host namespace including host-networking pods; pod B's traffic to a location outside the cluster is not covered.
Neither flow is covered, because host policies apply only to the node's own host namespace and never to any pod.
Only pod B's traffic is covered, because host policies explicitly exclude host-networking pods from the host namespace.

questions.explanation: A host policy is a CiliumClusterwideNetworkPolicy that uses a NodeSelector, and it applies to all the nodes that selector picks. Within each selected node, however, its scope is the host namespace, which expressly includes host-networking pods. Communications between non-host-networking pods and locations outside the cluster fall outside that scope, so pod B's flow is not governed by the host policy even though its node is selected.

optionRationale.a: Selecting the node is necessary but not sufficient: the policy's scope inside the node is the host namespace, so a pod in its own network namespace sending traffic outside the cluster is not covered.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt states that host policies apply to the host namespace 'including host-networking pods', so host-networking pod traffic is covered rather than excluded.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt says the opposite: host-networking pods are included in the host namespace, and it is non-host-networking pods talking to locations outside the cluster that are excluded.

citations.title: Host Policies
citations.quote: Host policies apply to all the nodes selected by their NodeSelector. In each selected node, they apply only to the host namespace, including host-networking pods. They don't apply to communications between non-host-networking pods and locations outside of the cluster.

questions.stem: An engineer has a LoadBalancer Service with spec.loadBalancerSourceRanges populated. By default the CIDR restrictions apply only to the LoadBalancer service, not to the NodePort and ClusterIP services created alongside it. The engineer wants those CIDRs to filter traffic for all externally exposed service types as well. Which action does the excerpt describe for this?

options.text: Enable bpf.lbSourceRangeAllTypes=true in Helm.
Add the annotation service.cilium.io/type: LoadBalancer to the Service.
Set service.cilium.io/src-ranges-policy to deny.
Remove spec.loadBalancerSourceRanges so that no restrictions are applied.

questions.explanation: The excerpt says that by default the white-listed CIDRs in spec.loadBalancerSourceRanges apply only to the LoadBalancer service, not to the corresponding NodePort or ClusterIP service. It then states that propagating the white-listed CIDRs to all externally exposed service types can be enabled in Helm via bpf.lbSourceRangeAllTypes=true.

optionRationale.b: The service.cilium.io/type: LoadBalancer annotation is described as a way to avoid the creation of corresponding NodePort and ClusterIP services, not as a way to propagate the CIDRs to them.
optionRationale.c: Setting service.cilium.io/src-ranges-policy to deny turns the CIDR list into a deny-list; it does not propagate the list to the other service types.
optionRationale.d: Removing spec.loadBalancerSourceRanges would leave the field empty, and the excerpt says that if the field is empty, no restrictions for the access will be applied.

citations.title: LoadBalancer Source Ranges Checks
citations.quote: This option can be enabled in Helm via ``bpf.lbSourceRangeAllTypes=true``.

questions.stem: A platform team is rolling out Cilium on a new cluster and wants Pod-level rate limiting in place from the start. What is the default state of the bandwidth manager on a fresh installation, and what must they do?

options.text: It is enabled by default, so no action is needed beyond annotating Pods.
It is disabled by default on new installations, so Cilium must be installed with the bandwidth manager enabled.
It is enabled by default only when BPF Host Routing is also enabled.
It is disabled by default and can only be turned on by chaining the bandwidth CNI plugin.

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that the bandwidth manager is disabled by default on new installations, and that to install Cilium with it enabled you must install Cilium with the bandwidth manager enabled. Nothing in the excerpt makes it conditional on BPF Host Routing, and the bandwidth manager explicitly does not use CNI chaining.

optionRationale.a: The excerpt says the opposite: it is disabled by default on new installations.
optionRationale.c: BPF Host Routing is strongly recommended as a companion, but the excerpt does not make the default enablement conditional on it.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt says the bandwidth manager does not rely on CNI chaining and does not use the bandwidth CNI plugin.

citations.title: Bandwidth Manager
citations.quote: Cilium's bandwidth manager is disabled by default on new installations.

questions.stem: An engineer is asked why Cilium's bandwidth manager does not simply use the Kubernetes bandwidth CNI plugin. Which explanation matches the excerpt?

options.text: The bandwidth CNI plugin is based on EDT, which is less scalable than the TBF approach Cilium uses.
The bandwidth CNI plugin cannot be used with Kubernetes Pod annotations at all.
The bandwidth CNI plugin is based on TBF rather than EDT, and there are scalability concerns in particular for multi-queue network interfaces.
The bandwidth CNI plugin only works in tunneling mode, whereas Cilium needs direct routing.

questions.explanation: The excerpt explains that the bandwidth manager is natively integrated into Cilium and does not make use of the bandwidth CNI plugin, because of scalability concerns in particular for multi-queue network interfaces; that plugin is based on TBF (Token Bucket Filter) instead of EDT.

optionRationale.a: The comparison is inverted: the CNI plugin uses TBF, while Cilium uses EDT.
optionRationale.b: The excerpt does not say the CNI plugin is incompatible with annotations; its stated reason is scalability and its TBF basis.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt says bandwidth enforcement is supported for direct routing as well as tunneling mode, and gives no such limitation for the CNI plugin.

citations.title: Bandwidth Manager
citations.quote:
Due to scalability concerns in particular for multi-queue network
interfaces, it is not recommended to use the bandwidth CNI plugin which is
based on TBF (Token Bucket Filter) instead of EDT.

questions.stem: A colleague reports that after a key rotation, `XfrmInStateProtoError` errors are appearing. According to the excerpt, which of the following can cause this error?

options.text: The kernel decrypted a packet and then failed to look up the route for it
The key was updated without incrementing the SPI, also called `KEYID`
A received packet matched an XFRM state that is being deleted
Cilium dropped packets that would otherwise have left the node in plain-text

questions.explanation: The excerpt lists two causes for `XfrmInStateProtoError`: updating the key without incrementing the SPI (also called `KEYID`), and a mismatch between the anti-replay seq on the source node and the anti-reply oseq on the destination node. Both are fixed by properly performing a new key rotation.

optionRationale.a: This describes `XfrmFwdHdrError` and `XfrmInError`, which occur when the kernel fails to look up the route for a decrypted packet.
optionRationale.c: This describes `XfrmInStateInvalid`, which can happen when packets are received while an XFRM state is being deleted.
optionRationale.d: This describes `XfrmOutPolBlock`, where Cilium dropped packets that would otherwise have left the node in plain-text.

citations.title: Troubleshooting
citations.quote:
``XfrmInStateProtoError`` errors can happen for the following reasons:
   1. If the key is updated without incrementing the SPI (also called ``KEYID``
   in ipsec_key_rotation instructions above).

questions.stem: After setting `service.cilium.io/affinity=local` in cluster 1, an engineer inspects endpoints with `cilium-dbg service list --clustermesh-affinity`. How are the local endpoints shown?

options.text: Marked as `(preferred)`.
Marked as `(active)` only, with no preference marker.
Removed from the list entirely.
Marked as `(unhealthy)`.

questions.explanation: Step 4 of the excerpt says that from cluster 1 the local endpoints are marked as preferred, and the sample output shows `(active) (preferred)` entries.

optionRationale.b: The `(active)` marker appears on all backends; the distinguishing marker for this case is `(preferred)`.
optionRationale.c: The endpoints remain listed; they are annotated with a preference marker.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt does not use an `(unhealthy)` marker in this output.

citations.title: Enabling Global Service Affinity
citations.quote:
From cluster 1, check the service endpoints, the local endpoints are marked
   as preferred.

questions.stem: After the L7 policy is in place, an engineer runs `kubectl exec xwing -- curl -s -XPOST deathstar.default.svc.cluster.local/v1/request-landing` and receives no response. Why?

options.text: The L7 rule permits only POST /v1/request-landing, so xwing's request is rejected with `Access denied`.
Because the rule builds on the identity-aware rule, traffic from pods without the label org=empire continues to be dropped, causing the connection to time out.
The path matches the exact URL, so xwing must use the regular expression /v1/.* instead.
xwing is calling port 80 over TCP, which the policy does not list in its toPorts section.

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that the L7 rule builds on the identity-aware rule, so traffic from pods without the label org=empire continues to be dropped, which causes the connection to time out.

optionRationale.a: `Access denied` is the L7 response given to tiefighter for a disallowed call; xwing never reaches the L7 stage because it lacks the required identity label.
optionRationale.c: The note about exact path matching and the /v1/.* regular expression concerns which URLs are allowed, not the identity-based drop applied to xwing.
optionRationale.d: Port 80 with protocol TCP is the port listed in the policy's toPorts section, so this is not the reason.

citations.title: Apply and Test HTTP-aware L7 Policy
citations.quote:
As this rule builds on the identity-aware rule, traffic from pods without the label
``org=empire`` will continue to be dropped causing the connection to time out

questions.stem: A Cilium datapath designer wants a BPF program that inspects packet data at the earliest possible moment after reception, before any other networking-stack processing, so that malicious traffic can be dropped with the best possible performance. Which BPF hook should the program be attached to?

options.text: The XDP hook
The traffic control ingress hook
The socket operations hook
The socket send/recv hook

questions.explanation: XDP sits at the earliest point in the networking driver and runs the program upon packet reception, directly on the packet data before any other processing, which the excerpt describes as the best possible packet processing performance and ideal for filtering programs that drop malicious or unexpected traffic.

optionRationale.c: The socket operations hook is attached to a cgroup and runs on TCP events, not on packet reception in the driver.
optionRationale.d: The socket send/recv hook runs on every send operation performed by a TCP socket, which is far removed from packet reception.

questions.stem: A LoadBalancer Service named hello-world initially carries only the label app=hello-world, and two advertisements select on vpc1=true and vpc2=true respectively. What is the BGP advertisement state for this Service at that point?

options.text: It is advertised with the communities of the first advertisement only.
It is advertised with the communities of both advertisements.
It is not advertised at all, because neither selector matches.
It is advertised without any communities attached.

questions.explanation: With no vpc1 or vpc2 label present, neither selector matches, which results in no matches and no BGP advertisements.

optionRationale.a: There is no match to begin with, so no advertisement is produced.
optionRationale.b: Both selectors require labels the Service does not yet have.
optionRationale.d: An unmatched Service is not advertised at all, rather than advertised bare.

attachments.title: The two advertisements
attachments.body:
apiVersion: cilium.io/v2
 kind: CiliumBGPAdvertisement
 metadata:
   name: bgp-advertisements
   labels:
     advertise: bgp
 spec:
   advertisements:
     - advertisementType: "Service"
       service:
         addresses:
           - LoadBalancerIP
       selector:
         matchExpressions:
           - { key: vpc1, operator: In, values: [ "true" ] }
       attributes:

questions.stem: A platform team wants `cilium monitor` to show DNS query names and HTTP request URLs for traffic leaving pods in the `default` namespace, rather than only packet-level events. Which change achieves this?

options.text: Create a `CiliumNetworkPolicy` with L7 rules for the relevant ports, which causes matching flows to be redirected to the proxy.
Restart the Cilium agent with L3/L4 event reporting disabled so that only application-layer events remain.
Add a `matchPattern` entry to the `endpointSelector` of an existing L3/L4 policy.
Run `hubble observe` with the `-t l7` filter, which upgrades captured L3/L4 events into L7 flow details.

questions.explanation: By default the monitor gives visibility only into L3/L4 packet events. To obtain L7 visibility you create a `CiliumNetworkPolicy` that specifies L7 rules; flows matching an L7 rule become visible to Cilium and are redirected to the proxy, so `cilium monitor` or `hubble observe` shows the L7 flow details. Note that such a policy also restricts traffic, so it is not a pure observation tool.

optionRationale.b: Nothing in the excerpt describes disabling L3/L4 reporting; the documented route to L7 visibility is an L7 policy.
optionRationale.c: `matchPattern` belongs under the `dns` rules of a `toPorts` entry, not inside `endpointSelector`, and the selector does not create L7 visibility.
optionRationale.d: The `-t l7` filter selects L7 flows for display; it does not itself produce L7 details, which require the traffic to be proxied by an L7 policy.

questions.stem: An engineer applies the policy below to pods in the `default` namespace. A pod then attempts an HTTP request to an endpoint in the `default` namespace on TCP port 9090. What is the result?

options.text: The request is dropped, because the policy restricts egress and nothing matches the L4 section of either rule.
The request is allowed and appears in `hubble observe` output as an L7 HTTP flow.
The request is allowed but only L3/L4 details are shown, since port 9090 has no L7 rule.
The request is proxied and allowed, because `http: [{}]` matches all ports for endpoints in the `default` namespace.

questions.explanation: The policy restricts egress communication and drops anything that is not matched. The HTTP rule covers only ports TCP/80 and TCP/8080, so traffic to port 9090 matches neither the DNS rule nor the HTTP rule and is dropped.

optionRationale.b: Only traffic on the ports named in the `toPorts` sections is picked up and proxied; port 9090 is not among them.
optionRationale.c: Unmatched egress is dropped rather than allowed, so there is no flow to observe at all.
optionRationale.d: The `http: [{}]` rules apply only to the ports listed in the same `toPorts` entry, namely 80 and 8080.

options.text: The DNS traffic to `kube-dns` on port 53 was redirected to the proxy and forwarded, which is why the L7 query details are visible.
The DNS traffic bypassed the proxy and was forwarded directly by the datapath, with the query details reconstructed afterwards.
The DNS response was dropped by the proxy after the query was forwarded.
The DNS traffic was forwarded by the kernel's connection tracker without involving Cilium.

questions.stem: A cluster-wide policy named default-deny is applied. It selects every endpoint whose io.kubernetes.pod.namespace is not kube-system, and its only egress rule permits UDP port 53 to the kube-dns endpoints in kube-system with a DNS matchPattern of '*'. A client outside the cluster then requests the /details endpoint of an application exposed through Cilium Ingress. What is the result?

options.text: The request is denied, and the response returned to the client is HTTP 403.
The request is allowed, because the policy contains no ingress section and therefore only restricts egress.
The request is allowed, because the reserved:ingress identity is excluded from the endpointSelector.
The request is dropped at the TCP layer, so the client receives no HTTP response at all.

questions.explanation: The policy denies all traffic by default, and the excerpt states that with it applied the request to /details is denied for external and in-cluster traffic. The captured session shows the client receiving an HTTP 403 Forbidden with server: envoy, so the denial is surfaced as an HTTP response rather than a silent connection failure.

optionRationale.b: The policy is described as blocking all traffic by default; the absence of an ingress section does not leave ingress unrestricted, and the observed result is a denial.
optionRationale.c: The endpointSelector excludes only the kube-system namespace; nothing in the policy exempts the reserved:ingress identity, which is handled by a separate policy later in the flow.
optionRationale.d: The captured output shows a complete HTTP exchange ending in 403 Forbidden, not a dropped connection.

attachments.title: The default-deny policy
attachments.body:
---
apiVersion: cilium.io/v2
kind: CiliumClusterwideNetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: "default-deny"
spec:
  description: "Block all the traffic (except DNS) by default"
  egress:
  - toEndpoints:
    - matchLabels:
        io.kubernetes.pod.namespace: kube-system
        k8s-app: kube-dns
    toPorts:
    - ports:
      - port: '53'
        protocol: UDP
      rules:
        dns:
        - matchPattern: '*'
  endpointSelector:
    matchExpressions:
    - key: io.kubernetes.pod.namespace
      operator: NotIn
      values:
      - kube-system

questions.stem: After a default-deny policy has blocked traffic to an application behind Cilium Ingress, a second CiliumClusterwideNetworkPolicy named allow-ingress-egress is applied. It selects endpoints for which reserved:ingress exists and allows egress to the cluster entity. What effect does this have?

options.text: It allows the ingress proxy to reach endpoints in the cluster, so requests to /details succeed from both an external client and an in-cluster client.
It allows only external traffic, because the cluster entity covers endpoints outside the cluster rather than inside it.
It has no effect until the default-deny policy is deleted, because cluster-wide policies are evaluated in creation order.
It allows the ingress proxy to reach the cluster, but in-cluster clients remain blocked because they do not carry the reserved:ingress identity.

questions.explanation: The policy grants egress from the reserved:ingress identity to all cluster identities, and the captured session shows both the external curl and the in-cluster client from deployment/client receiving the /details payload. The excerpt notes that allowing all traffic from reserved:ingress to all cluster identities is generally the more reliable option, since Cilium Ingress is part of the networking infrastructure.

optionRationale.b: The policy targets the cluster entity, and the excerpt's own output shows the in-cluster client succeeding, so the rule is not limited to external traffic.
optionRationale.c: Nothing in the excerpt describes creation-order evaluation or a requirement to delete the default-deny policy first; the allow policy takes effect alongside it.
optionRationale.d: The captured output shows the in-cluster client from deployment/client receiving the same JSON payload, so in-cluster traffic is no longer blocked.

    matchExpressions:

questions.stem: A cluster runs the CiliumEgressGatewayPolicy shown in the attachment. A pod with labels org=empire and class=mediabot in the default namespace is scheduled on node1 and sends traffic to an external address. What happens to that traffic?

options.text: It is routed through node2 and SNATed with the egress IP 10.168.60.100.
It is SNATed on node1 using the first IPv4 address of the interface enp0s8.
It leaves the cluster without SNAT because the destination 0.0.0.0/0 is not matched by the policy.
It is dropped because the pod is not on the gateway node.

questions.explanation: The policy selects pods with org=empire and class=mediabot in the default namespace, and its nodeSelector restricts it to node1. Traffic from those pods on node1 to 0.0.0.0/0 or ::/0 is routed through the gateway node labelled node.kubernetes.io/name: node2, which SNATs it with the egress IP 10.168.60.100.

optionRationale.b: The interface field is only an alternative to egressIP; here egressIP is set, so the interface is not used.
optionRationale.c: The policy explicitly lists 0.0.0.0/0 and ::/0 as destinationCIDRs, so all traffic leaving the cluster is matched.
optionRationale.d: The policy routes traffic through the gateway node; it does not drop traffic from pods on other nodes.

attachments.title: The egress gateway policy under test
attachments.body:
apiVersion: cilium.io/v2
kind: CiliumEgressGatewayPolicy
metadata:
  name: egress-sample
spec:
  # Specify which pods should be subject to the current policy.
  # Multiple pod selectors can be specified.
  selectors:
  - podSelector:
      matchLabels:
        org: empire
        class: mediabot
        # The following label selects default namespace
        io.kubernetes.pod.namespace: default
    nodeSelector: # optional, if not specified the policy applies to all nodes
      matchLabels:
        node.kubernetes.io/name: node1 # only traffic from this node will be SNATed
  # Specify which destination CIDR(s) this policy applies to.
  # Multiple CIDRs can be specified.
  destinationCIDRs:
  - "0.0.0.0/0"
  - "::/0"

  # Configure the gateway node.
  egressGateway:
    # Specify which node should act as gateway for this policy.
    nodeSelector:
      matchLabels:
        node.kubernetes.io/name: node2

    # Specify the IP address used to SNAT traffic matched by the policy.
    # It must exist as an IP associated with a network interface on the instance.
    egressIP: 10.168.60.100

    # Alternatively it's possible to specify the interface to be used for egress traffic.
    # In this case the first IPv4 and IPv6 addresses assigned to that interface will be used
    # as egress IP.
    # interface: enp0s8

citations.title: Example policy
citations.quote:
Creating the ``CiliumEgressGatewayPolicy`` resource above would cause all
traffic originating from pods with the ``org: empire`` and ``class: mediabot``
labels in the ``default`` namespace on node ``node1`` and destined to ``0.0.0.0/0`` or ``::/0``
(i.e. all traffic leaving the cluster) to be routed through the gateway node with the
``node.kubernetes.io/name: node2`` label, which will then SNAT said
traffic with the ``10.168.60.100`` egress IP.

questions.stem: An engineer enables graceful restart on a CiliumBGPPeerConfig but does not set restartTimeSeconds. A Cilium Agent then restarts. How long does the peering router wait, by default, before removing the routes previously advertised by the Cilium BGP control plane?

options.text: 120 seconds
15 seconds
Until the Cilium Agent sends a new BGP OPEN message, with no timer involved
The routes are withdrawn immediately, because no RestartTime was configured

questions.explanation: The excerpt gives the default explicitly: the default value of RestartTime is 120 seconds. The timer starts when the peer receives the TCP FIN and moves to Idle, and the routes are removed when it expires.

optionRationale.b: 15 seconds appears only in the example manifest as an explicitly configured restartTimeSeconds value, not as a default.
optionRationale.c: The peer starts its RestartTime timer on receiving the TCP FIN; the wait is bounded by that timer rather than by the next OPEN message.
optionRationale.d: Graceful restart is what prevents immediate withdrawal; the default timer still applies when restartTimeSeconds is omitted.

questions.stem: A Cilium Agent managing BGP peering is restarted. The peering router receives a TCP FIN on the BGP session. What does the router do, and what happens to traffic in the datapath while the Agent restarts?

options.text: It changes its BGP state to Idle and starts its RestartTime timer, while the datapath continues to forward traffic with no disruption.
It immediately withdraws all routes learned from Cilium, and forwarding stops until the Agent reconnects.
It keeps the session in Established state and ignores the FIN until a new BGP OPEN message arrives.
It changes its BGP state to Idle and starts its RestartTime timer, but the datapath drops traffic until the session is re-established.

questions.explanation: On receiving the TCP FIN the peer changes its BGP state to Idle and starts its RestartTime timer. Because the peering router does not withdraw the routes immediately and the datapath continues to forward traffic during the Agent restart, there is no traffic disruption.

optionRationale.b: Immediate withdrawal is exactly what graceful restart avoids; the peer waits for the RestartTime timer instead.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt states the peer changes its BGP state to Idle on receiving the TCP FIN, so it does not stay in Established.
optionRationale.d: The state transition and timer are right, but the excerpt states the datapath continues to forward traffic during Agent restart, so there is no disruption.

starts its ``RestartTime`` timer.

questions.stem: A cluster's Cilium Agent takes roughly 40 seconds to boot after a restart. You want the peering BGP router to keep the routes it learned from the Cilium BGP control plane for as long as possible during that restart, but you also want the peer to remove them if the Agent fails to come back. Which configuration should you apply?

options.text: A CiliumBGPPeerConfig with `gracefulRestart.enabled: true` and `restartTimeSeconds: 15`
A CiliumBGPPeerConfig with `gracefulRestart.enabled: true` and `restartTimeSeconds: 60`
A CiliumBGPPeerConfig with `gracefulRestart.enabled: false` and `restartTimeSeconds: 60`
A CiliumBGPPeerConfig with `gracefulRestart.enabled: true` and no `restartTimeSeconds`, relying on the 120-second default

questions.explanation: `RestartTime` is the time advertised to the peer within which the Cilium BGP control plane is expected to re-establish the BGP session after a restart, and on its expiration the peer removes the routes previously advertised. Because the Agent here needs about 40 seconds to boot, the value must be greater than that boot time, so 60 seconds is the suitable choice. A value of 15 seconds would expire before the Agent is back, and the default of 120 seconds is not the tightest fit for the stated requirement.

optionRationale.a: 15 seconds is shorter than the roughly 40-second boot time, so the peer's timer would expire and the routes would be removed before the session is re-established.
optionRationale.c: Graceful restart must be enabled for the capability to be advertised and for the peer to hold routes; disabling it defeats the purpose.
optionRationale.d: The 120-second default is valid, but the question asks for the setting that keeps routes only as long as needed while still covering the boot time, which 60 seconds does more precisely.

   name: cilium-peer
 spec:
   gracefulRestart:
     enabled: true
     restartTimeSeconds: 15

questions.stem: A cluster runs in Multi-Pool IPAM mode. A pod is created in a namespace that carries the annotation ipam.cilium.io/ip-pool=green-pool, while the pod itself carries the annotation ipam.cilium.io/ip-pool=blue-pool. Both pools exist and both have selectors that would match the pod. Which pool is the pod's IP allocated from?

options.text: blue-pool, because the annotation on the pod takes precedence over the annotation on the namespace
green-pool, because the namespace annotation is evaluated first
The default pool, because conflicting annotations are ignored
Allocation fails, because the pod matches more than one pool

questions.explanation: The explicit pool annotation is the first item in the precedence order, and it may be placed either on the pod or on the namespace of the pod. The pod's own annotation is the one that names the pool, so blue-pool is used; the namespace annotation does not override it.

optionRationale.b: The namespace annotation is an alternative place to put the explicit pool name, not a higher-priority source than the pod's own annotation.
optionRationale.c: The default pool is only used when neither the pod nor the namespace has an explicit pool annotation, or when no selectors match.
optionRationale.d: The exactly-one-pool rule applies to matching pools via selectors; here the pool is named explicitly by annotation.

citations.title: Architecture
citations.quote:
You can explicitly name the pool for a pod using the ``ipam.cilium.io/ip-pool=<pool-name>`` annotation, 
     either on the pod or the namespace of the pod.

options.text: Allocation fails; set ipam.cilium.io/require-pool-match="true" to allow the default pool as a fallback
The pod is allocated an IP from the default pool; set ipam.cilium.io/require-pool-match="true" on the pod or namespace to block allocation until a non-default pool matches
The pod is allocated an IP from the default pool; set spec.allowFirstIP to true on the pool to prevent this
The pod is allocated an IP from the default pool; nothing can change this behaviour

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that when the pool is not known to Cilium at allocation time, whether from race conditions or misconfiguration, the pod receives an IP from the default pool. The require-pool-match annotation blocks allocation until the pod matches a non-default pool.

optionRationale.a: Allocation does not fail in this case; it falls back to the default pool, and require-pool-match blocks rather than permits the fallback.
optionRationale.c: allowFirstIP controls whether the first address of an allocated CIDR is allocatable; it has nothing to do with pool selection.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt explicitly offers require-pool-match as a way to change this behaviour.

In the case that your pool is not known to Cilium at the time of IP allocation, either due to race conditions or

The change has no effect, because the annotations are only considered when a pod is created
The change causes IP allocation to fail and an error to be logged

optionRationale.a: No re-allocation occurs for a running pod.
optionRationale.b: The excerpt gives no such restart behaviour; the annotation simply has no effect on the running pod.
optionRationale.d: An error is logged when a pod matches more than one pool, not when an annotation is changed on a running pod.

questions.stem: A cluster runs in Multi-Pool IPAM mode. A pod is created in a namespace that carries the annotation ipam.cilium.io/ip-pool=blue-pool, but the pod itself carries the annotation ipam.cilium.io/ip-pool=green-pool. Both pools exist and both have free addresses. Which pool is the pod's IP allocated from?

options.text: green-pool, because the annotation on the pod takes precedence over the annotation on its namespace
blue-pool, because the namespace annotation is evaluated before the pod annotation
The default pool, because conflicting annotations cause the explicit pool selection to be ignored
Neither pool: allocation fails because the pod matches two pools

questions.explanation: The explicit pool annotation is the first item in the precedence order, and it may be placed either on the pod or on the namespace of the pod. The pod's own annotation is the one that names the pool for that pod, so green-pool is used. The failure case for matching more than one pool concerns label selectors, not annotations: a pod must match exactly one pool for a given IP family, and overlapping selectors are what cause allocation to fail.

optionRationale.b: The namespace annotation is an alternative place to put the explicit pool name, not an earlier step in the precedence order; the pod's own annotation names the pool.
optionRationale.c: Nothing in the precedence order makes conflicting annotations fall back to the default pool; the default pool is used only when there is no explicit annotation and no selector match.
optionRationale.d: The 'exactly one pool' rule applies to matching pools via selectors; overlapping selectors are what make allocation fail, not an annotation on the pod.

questions.stem: An operator is creating a CiliumPodIPPool with a /24 IPv4 CIDR and wants the very first address of that CIDR to be handed out to pods rather than reserved. Which field must be set to true when the pool is created?

options.text: spec.allowFirstIP
spec.allowLastIP
spec.ipv4.maskSize
spec.ipam.pools.requested

questions.explanation: By default the first and last address of each allocated CIDR from a CiliumPodIPPool are reserved. Note that this field, like spec.allowLastIP, is immutable, so it must be set at creation time.

optionRationale.b: spec.allowLastIP controls the last address of the CIDR, not the first.
optionRationale.c: maskSize sets the size of the per-node PodCIDRs carved from the pool; it does not control whether the first address is reserved.
optionRationale.d: spec.ipam.pools.requested is a field of the CiliumNode resource listing per-node pool requests, not a field of CiliumPodIPPool.

citations.title: Architecture

``CiliumPodIPPool`` are reserved and cannot be allocated. Set
``spec.allowFirstIP`` or ``spec.allowLastIP`` to ``true`` when creating the pool

questions.stem: An engineer sets `connectRetryTimeSeconds: 5` on a BGP peer configuration to speed up reconnection after losing connectivity. What range of values can the actual ConnectRetryTimer take?

optionRationale.c: The interval starts at the configured value, not below it; jitter is not subtracted.
optionRationale.d: The upper bound of the interval is exclusive, and the value is not fixed at double the configured value.

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that Cilium provides the `--hubble-redact-enabled` option, which enables Hubble to handle sensitive information present in Layer 7 flows. The other options select particular categories of data to redact for supported protocols.

optionRationale.b: This option redacts URL query (GET) parameters; it is one of the per-protocol features, not the enabling switch.
optionRationale.c: This option defines the headers exempt from header redaction; it does not enable redaction overall.

questions.stem: An engineer needs to redact only a specific, named set of HTTP headers while leaving all other headers visible in Layer 7 flows. Which option fits, and how does it differ from the alternative header option?

options.text: `--hubble-redact-http-headers-deny`, which redacts only the headers defined in its list, whereas the allow option redacts all headers except those listed.
`--hubble-redact-http-headers-allow`, which redacts only the headers defined in its list, whereas the deny option redacts all headers except those listed.
`--hubble-redact-http-urlquery`, which redacts named headers as well as query parameters.
`--hubble-redact-enabled`, which redacts a fixed set of headers chosen by Hubble.

questions.explanation: The excerpt offers two header modes: redacting all headers except those in the `--hubble-redact-http-headers-allow` list, or redacting only the headers in the `--hubble-redact-http-headers-deny` list. To redact only a named set, the deny list is the correct choice.

optionRationale.b: This swaps the two modes; the allow list preserves the named headers and redacts the rest.
optionRationale.c: `--hubble-redact-http-urlquery` concerns URL query (GET) parameters, not headers.
optionRationale.d: `--hubble-redact-enabled` is the option that enables Hubble to handle sensitive information; the excerpt does not describe it as redacting a fixed set of headers.

questions.stem: An engineer proposes joining a production cluster and a shared development cluster into one Cluster Mesh so that services can be reached across both. What does Cilium's security model say about this plan?

options.text: It is acceptable, because Cilium performs sanity checks on all information received from remote clusters and blocks malicious data.
It is acceptable, because each cluster keeps its own separate trust domain and policies are never shared.
It should be avoided, because all clusters in a Cluster Mesh form a single trust domain and should be mutually trusted with equivalent security postures.
It is acceptable, because the Cilium operator in each cluster re-validates every remote identity before use.

questions.explanation: Clusters joined in a Cluster Mesh share one trust domain, so the security posture of the weakest cluster matters to all of them. Cilium's sanity checks are not a substitute for trust: they cannot fully prevent a compromised cluster's control plane from propagating malicious information. Only mutually trusted clusters with equivalent security postures should be connected.

optionRationale.a: The sanity checks are explicitly described as unable to fully prevent a compromised cluster's control plane from propagating malicious information, so they are not a guarantee.
optionRationale.b: The opposite is true: all clusters connected in a Cluster Mesh form a single trust domain.
optionRationale.d: No such re-validation by the operator is described; the checks that exist are performed by Cilium and are not claimed to be sufficient.

questions.stem: A Cilium agent on one node needs to derive the identity for a set of labels. How does it obtain the identity?

options.text: It queries the distributed key-value store, which either creates a new identity or returns the identity from the initial query for that label set.
It asks the Hubble Relay, which assigns identities based on observed network flows.
It computes the identity locally from a hash of the labels, with no coordination with other nodes.
It reads the identity from the pod's Kubernetes ServiceAccount token.

questions.explanation: The endpoint identity is resolved with the help of the distributed key-value store, which supports the atomic operation of generating a new unique identifier only if the value has not been seen before. Depending on whether the label set was queried before, a new identity is created or the existing one is returned.

optionRationale.b: Hubble Relay is not involved in identity derivation; the excerpt attributes resolution to the distributed key-value store.
optionRationale.c: Local hashing would not require coordination between cluster nodes, which the excerpt says is required.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt makes no mention of ServiceAccount tokens; identity is derived from the identity-relevant label subset.

distributed key-value store which allows to perform atomic operations in the

before*.

questions.stem: Why does cluster-wide identity sharing require coordination between cluster nodes?

options.text: Because each node must broadcast its pod list to every other node on every scheduling event.
Because identities must be unique per node so that traffic can be routed back to the correct endpoint.
Because a single identity must be agreed across nodes, which the distributed key-value store provides through atomic create-if-not-seen operations.
Because the CNI plugin must be reinstalled on each node whenever a new identity is created.

questions.explanation: Since identities are valid in the entire cluster, nodes must agree on them. The distributed key-value store allows the atomic operation of generating a new unique identifier if the value has not been seen before, so each node can derive the same identity for the same label subset.

optionRationale.a: The excerpt describes coordination through the key-value store, not broadcasting pod lists between nodes.
optionRationale.b: Identities are shared across nodes rather than unique per node, which is precisely why coordination is needed.
optionRationale.d: Nothing in the excerpt links identity creation to CNI reinstallation.

questions.stem: A platform team wants Cilium to derive identities from the labels `team.payments` and `team.search` on their pods, while ignoring labels such as `deploy-timestamp`. Which label prefix must they configure when starting the agent?

options.text: `team.`
`id.`
`deploy-timestamp`
`labels.`

questions.explanation: Cilium derives identities only from labels whose names start with one of the configured meaningful prefixes. To make `team.payments` and `team.search` security relevant, the prefix `team.` must be in that list. The default prefix `id.` would not match them, and `deploy-timestamp` is exactly the kind of metadata label that should be excluded.

optionRationale.b: `id.` is the standard default prefix, so it would not capture labels beginning with `team.`.
optionRationale.c: `deploy-timestamp` is the metadata label the team wants ignored, not a prefix to make meaningful.
optionRationale.d: `labels.` is not a prefix used by these pods and would match nothing here.

questions.stem: A cluster runs the Cilium agent with `enable-policy: always`. A pod has no CiliumNetworkPolicy selecting it in either direction. What happens to traffic to and from that pod?

options.text: All traffic is allowed, because no rule selects the pod.
Policy enforcement applies to the pod even though no rules select it, so only traffic permitted by policy is allowed.
Policy enforcement is disabled on the pod, so all traffic is allowed from any source or to any destination.
Ingress is enforced but egress is unrestricted until an egress rule selects the pod.

questions.explanation: In `always` mode, policy enforcement is enabled on all endpoints even if no rules select specific endpoints. The absence of a selecting policy therefore does not leave the pod open.

optionRationale.a: This describes `default` mode, where endpoints have unrestricted network access until selected by policy.
optionRationale.c: This describes `never` mode, where enforcement is disabled on all endpoints even if rules select them.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt does not describe a mode that enforces one direction only by default; the per-direction behaviour belongs to `default` mode.

questions.stem: A team wants pods labelled app=myService to reach the external IP 20.1.1.1 and the whole 10.0.0.0/8 range, but never 10.96.0.0/12. Which egress rule set achieves this?

options.text: One egress rule with toCIDR: 20.1.1.1/32 and a second egress rule with toCIDRSet using cidr: 10.0.0.0/8 and except: 10.96.0.0/12
A single egress rule with toCIDRSet listing 20.1.1.1/32, 10.0.0.0/8 and 10.96.0.0/12
One egress rule with toCIDR: 10.0.0.0/8 and a second egress rule with toCIDRSet using cidr: 20.1.1.1/32 and except: 10.96.0.0/12
A single egress rule with toCIDR: 20.1.1.1/32 and toCIDRSet: 10.0.0.0/8, with 10.96.0.0/12 listed under except on the toCIDR entry

questions.explanation: The policy separates the two intents: a plain toCIDR entry allows the single external IP 20.1.1.1/32, and a toCIDRSet entry allows 10.0.0.0/8 while carving out 10.96.0.0/12 with except. Each egress item is its own rule, so the IP and the CIDR set are expressed separately.

optionRationale.b: Listing 10.96.0.0/12 alongside the allowed ranges would permit it rather than exclude it; the exclusion must be expressed with except.
optionRationale.c: The CIDR set with the except clause is attached to the wrong range here, so the carve-out would apply to the single IP instead of 10.0.0.0/8.
optionRationale.d: toCIDR and toCIDRSet are separate fields on separate rules; except belongs to the toCIDRSet entry, not to a toCIDR entry.

kind: CiliumNetworkPolicy

  - toCIDRSet:
    - cidr: 10.0.0.0/8
      except:
      - 10.96.0.0/12

questions.stem: After the policy shown is applied, a pod labelled app=myService tries to connect to 10.96.5.5. What is the result?

options.text: The connection is denied, because 10.96.0.0/12 is excluded from the allowed 10.0.0.0/8 range
The connection is allowed, because 10.96.5.5 falls inside 10.0.0.0/8
The connection is allowed, because the except list only applies to ingress traffic
The connection is denied, because only the single IP 20.1.1.1/32 is permitted for egress

questions.explanation: The toCIDRSet entry allows 10.0.0.0/8 but lists 10.96.0.0/12 under except, so addresses inside that excluded prefix are not permitted even though they sit within the broader range. 10.96.5.5 is inside 10.96.0.0/12 and is therefore denied.

optionRationale.b: Being inside 10.0.0.0/8 is not sufficient, because the except clause removes 10.96.0.0/12 from the allowed set.
optionRationale.c: The except list is part of the egress toCIDRSet rule and has nothing to do with ingress.
optionRationale.d: The policy also allows 10.0.0.0/8 through the toCIDRSet rule, so egress is not limited to the single IP.

questions.stem: You run `cilium clustermesh status --context $CLUSTER1 --wait` and the command keeps printing lines such as `⌛ Waiting (25s) for clusters to be connected: 2 nodes are not ready`. What is the command doing?

options.text: It is blocking until the clusters are connected, reporting how many nodes are not yet ready.
It has failed permanently because two nodes are unreachable and must be deleted.
It is waiting for the LoadBalancer service to be assigned an IP address.
It is waiting for the Cilium agents on the local cluster to be scheduled.

questions.explanation: With `--wait`, the command keeps polling and prints progress lines showing how many nodes are not yet ready, until all nodes are connected to all clusters. The repeated `⌛ Waiting` lines are progress output, not a terminal failure.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt shows the wait progressing from 2 nodes not ready to 1, then completing successfully, so it is not a permanent failure.
optionRationale.c: The LoadBalancer wait is reported separately, as `Service "clustermesh-apiserver" of type "LoadBalancer" found`; the `Waiting ... for clusters to be connected` line is about node connectivity.
optionRationale.d: The message concerns nodes not being connected to clusters, not local agent scheduling.

questions.stem: The validation output ends with `✅ All 2 nodes are connected to all clusters [min:1 / avg:1.0 / max:1]` followed by a `🔌 Cluster Connections:` list showing `2/2 configured, 2/2 connected`. What does this tell you?

options.text: Every node in the cluster is connected to every remote cluster, and the remote cluster's nodes are all configured and connected.
Only one node in the cluster is connected, so the mesh is partially degraded.
The remote cluster is configured but not yet connected.
The LoadBalancer has not yet been assigned an IP, so the connection count is provisional.

questions.explanation: The success line reports that all nodes are connected to all clusters, with the minimum, average and maximum connection counts all at 1 or above. The connection list then shows the remote cluster as fully configured and fully connected.

optionRationale.b: The `min:1` figure is the minimum number of cluster connections per node, not a count of connected nodes; the line states all nodes are connected.
optionRationale.c: The list shows `2/2 connected`, so the remote cluster is connected, not merely configured.
optionRationale.d: The LoadBalancer assignment is reported earlier in the output as a separate check, and the connection counts here are final.
