questions.stem: An engineer wants to attach a label to a set of endpoints so that a policy can select them by key alone, without caring about any value. Which label format should be used?

options.text: `io.cilium.mykey=myvalue`
`io.cilium.mykey`
`mykey=io.cilium`
`io.cilium.mykey=`

questions.explanation: The value portion of a label is optional and can be omitted entirely, leaving just the key, for example `io.cilium.mykey`. The key is the mandatory part; the value need not be supplied.

optionRationale.a: This is the full key=value form, which supplies a value rather than omitting it.
optionRationale.c: This reverses the intended order, putting the value-like portion first and the reverse-domain key second.
optionRationale.d: This still supplies a value, albeit an empty one, rather than omitting the value portion.

citations.title: What is a Label?
citations.quote: The value portion is optional and can be omitted, e.g. ``io.cilium.mykey``.

questions.stem: A label is described as a pair of strings. Which statement correctly describes the two portions?

options.text: Both the key and the value are mandatory.
The value is mandatory and the key is optional.
The key is mandatory and must be unique, while the value is optional.
Neither portion is mandatory, but both must be unique.

questions.explanation: A label consists of a key and a value. The key portion is mandatory and must be unique, whereas the value portion is optional and can be omitted.

optionRationale.a: Only the key is mandatory; the value can be omitted.
optionRationale.b: This reverses the roles — the key is the mandatory portion, not the value.
optionRationale.d: The key is mandatory, and uniqueness is required of the key, not of both portions.

citations.title: What is a Label?
citations.quote: The key portion is mandatory and must be unique.

questions.stem: A cluster runs CoreDNS in the kube-system namespace with the service account coredns. Cilium has just been installed and the kvstore is not yet reachable. What does Cilium do when it first sees these DNS pods?

options.text: It assigns identity 104 automatically, without contacting the kvstore.
It assigns identity 102 automatically, without contacting the kvstore.
It waits for the kvstore to become reachable before assigning any identity.
It assigns identity 106 automatically, without contacting the kvstore.

questions.explanation: CoreDNS in kube-system with the coredns service account is a well-known identity with numeric ID 104, and well-known identities are handed out automatically without contacting external dependencies such as the kvstore. This is what allows policy enforcement for essential services during bootstrap.

optionRationale.b: 102 is the numeric ID of the kube-dns deployment, not of core-dns.
optionRationale.c: The whole point of well-known identities is that they are allocated without any external dependency, so no kvstore wait is needed.
optionRationale.d: 106 is the numeric ID for core-dns on EKS, which carries the additional eks.amazonaws.com/component=coredns label; the plain core-dns entry is 104.

citations.title: Well-known Identities
citations.quote:
automatically and will hand out a security identity without requiring to
contact any external dependencies such as the kvstore.

questions.stem: A team creates a Service annotated with service.cilium.io/global: "true" and does not set any other Cilium annotation. What is the resulting load-balancing behaviour across the clusters in the Cluster Mesh?

options.text: Backends are load-balanced across multiple clusters, because sharing is implicitly enabled.
Only local backends are used, because sharing must be opted into explicitly.
The Service is rejected by the agent until service.cilium.io/shared is set.
Backends are shared only with clusters that carry a matching service.cilium.io/shared annotation.

questions.explanation: A Global Service load-balances across backends in multiple clusters by default, and this implicitly configures service.cilium.io/shared: "true". No further annotation is needed to enable sharing.

optionRationale.b: Sharing is the default for a Global Service, not something that must be opted into.
optionRationale.c: Nothing in the behaviour described requires the shared annotation to be set explicitly; it is configured implicitly.
optionRationale.d: Sharing is not gated on a matching annotation in the other clusters.

questions.stem: After the policy below is applied, a client in another cluster can still reach the rebel-base Service, but clients in other clusters no longer see this cluster's rebel-base pods as backends. Which annotation in the manifest produces that effect?

options.text: service.cilium.io/shared: "false"
service.cilium.io/global: "true"
spec.type: ClusterIP
spec.selector: name: rebel-base

questions.explanation: The shared annotation set to "false" prevents this cluster's service backends from being shared to other clusters, while the global annotation keeps the Service global so remote endpoints are still exposed.

optionRationale.b: The global annotation makes the Service a Global Service; on its own it would also share local endpoints.
optionRationale.c: The Service type controls how the Service is exposed locally, not whether backends are shared across clusters.
optionRationale.d: The selector determines which pods are backends; it does not control cross-cluster sharing.

attachments.title: The policy under test
attachments.body:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: rebel-base
  annotations:
    service.cilium.io/global: "true"
    service.cilium.io/shared: "false"
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  ports:
  - port: 80
  selector:
    name: rebel-base

questions.stem: How do `toCIDR` and `toCIDRSet` differ in what they express about destination prefixes?

options.text: `toCIDR` allows an optional exclusion list of subnets; `toCIDRSet` does not.
`toCIDRSet` allows an optional exclusion list of subnets per destination prefix; `toCIDR` only lists allowed destination prefixes.
`toCIDR` applies to ingress while `toCIDRSet` applies to egress.
Both fields are identical apart from the name.

questions.explanation: `toCIDR` is simply a list of allowed destination prefixes/CIDRs, whereas `toCIDRSet` adds an optional list of subnets of the destination prefix/CIDR to which communication is not allowed.

optionRationale.a: The exclusion list belongs to `toCIDRSet`, not `toCIDR`.
optionRationale.c: Both fields describe destinations that selected endpoints are allowed to talk to, so both are egress-oriented.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt distinguishes them by the optional exclusion list in `toCIDRSet`.

optionRationale.d: The excerpt explicitly describes a way to overcome the limitation.

questions.stem: A platform team runs a StatefulSet called `my-statefulset` in two clusters that are joined in a Cluster Mesh, and both are governed by the same Service. EndpointSlice synchronisation is enabled. What does Cilium do with the hostnames from the two clusters?

options.text: It synchronises them as is, without any form of conflict resolution.
It detects the duplicate hostnames and renames one set by appending the cluster name.
It refuses to synchronise EndpointSlices until the StatefulSet names differ.
It keeps only the hostnames from the cluster with the lowest cluster ID.

questions.explanation: Hostnames are synchronised as is and no conflict resolution is performed, so identical StatefulSet names across clusters produce clashing hostnames. The documented workaround is to give the StatefulSets different names, for example by adding the cluster name.

optionRationale.b: Cilium does not rename anything; the excerpt states there is no conflict resolution mechanism, and the cluster-name prefix is a manual naming convention, not automatic behaviour.
optionRationale.c: Nothing in the excerpt says synchronisation is blocked; the hostnames are synchronised as is.
optionRationale.d: No tie-breaking by cluster ID is described; the excerpt explicitly says there is no conflict resolution.

citations.title: Known Limitations
citations.quote: Hostnames are synchronized as is without any form of conflict resolution

questions.stem: You are deploying a StatefulSet governed by a single Service across several clusters in a Cluster Mesh, with EndpointSlice synchronisation enabled. Which naming approach does the documentation recommend?

options.text: Use the same StatefulSet name in every cluster so the Service selects them uniformly.
Give each StatefulSet a different name, for example by adding the cluster name such as `cluster1-my-statefulset`.
Give each StatefulSet a different governing Service so hostnames cannot collide.
Disable EndpointSlice synchronisation for StatefulSets and rely on the global Service only.

questions.explanation: Because hostnames are synchronised as is with no conflict resolution, multiple StatefulSets with a single governing Service that synchronise EndpointSlices across clusters should have different names, for instance by prefixing the cluster name.

optionRationale.a: Identical names are exactly the case the excerpt warns against, since the hostnames would collide with no resolution mechanism.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt keeps a single governing Service and addresses the StatefulSet names instead.
optionRationale.d: Disabling synchronisation is not suggested; the excerpt recommends differentiating the StatefulSet names.

citations.title: Known Limitations
citations.quote: you can add the cluster name to the StatefulSet name

questions.stem: A security team wants to allow pods selected by a CiliumNetworkPolicy to communicate with all endpoints in the local cluster, including unmanaged endpoints and the host, but not with endpoints outside the cluster. Which entity should they use in the policy?

options.text: `cluster`
`world`
`all`
`cluster-mesh`

questions.explanation: The `cluster` entity is the logical group of all network endpoints inside the local cluster, including Cilium-managed endpoints, unmanaged endpoints, the host, remote-node, init, ingress, health, and kube-apiserver entities. It does not include endpoints outside the cluster, which are covered by `world`.

optionRationale.b: `world` corresponds to all endpoints outside the cluster and is identical to allowing CIDR 0.0.0.0/0, which is broader than required.
optionRationale.c: `all` represents the combination of all known clusters as well as world, so it would also allow external communication.
optionRationale.d: `cluster-mesh` selects all endpoints in meshed clusters as well as everything in the cluster entity, which includes remote clusters.

citations.title: Entities based
citations.quote:
Cluster is the logical group of all network endpoints inside of the local
    cluster. This includes all Cilium-managed endpoints of the local cluster,
    unmanaged endpoints in the local cluster, as well as the host,
    remote-node, init, ingress, health, and kube-apiserver entities.

questions.stem: A team wants pods labelled role=restricted to be unable to initiate any outbound connections, without naming any allowed destination. Which manifest achieves this?

options.text: A CiliumNetworkPolicy with endpointSelector matching role=restricted and an egress section containing a single empty rule `- {}`.
A CiliumNetworkPolicy with endpointSelector matching role=restricted and an ingress section containing a single empty rule `- {}`.
A CiliumNetworkPolicy with endpointSelector matching role=restricted and no ingress or egress rule sections at all.
A CiliumNetworkPolicy with endpointSelector matching role=restricted and an egress section listing an explicit toEndpoints peer for every other pod in the cluster.

questions.explanation: An endpoint enters default deny mode at egress when a rule selects it and contains an egress rule section. An empty egress rule (`- {}`) puts the endpoint into default deny mode without whitelisting any peers, so no outbound connection is permitted.

optionRationale.b: An empty ingress rule would put the endpoint into default deny mode at ingress, not egress, so outbound traffic would be unaffected.
optionRationale.c: A policy that selects the endpoint but contains neither an ingress nor an egress rule section does not put the endpoint into default deny mode.
optionRationale.d: Listing explicit peers whitelists those peers rather than denying all egress; the goal is to allow nothing.

attachments.title: The policy under test
attachments.body:
apiVersion: "cilium.io/v2"
kind: CiliumNetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: "deny-all-egress"
spec:
  endpointSelector:
    matchLabels:
      role: restricted
  egress:
  - {}

questions.stem: A team needs to allow a pod to reach a database server that runs on a VM outside the cluster and has no Kubernetes labels. Which policy approach fits this requirement?

options.text: A CIDR-based policy, because the destination cannot be mapped to an identity derived from endpoint labels.
An entity-based policy selecting the `world` entity, because external VMs are always covered by that entity.
A label-based policy using the VM's hostname as the label value.

questions.stem: An Ingress object defines two paths of type ImplementationSpecific: /impl and /impl.*. A client requests /impl. Which path handles the request, and why?

options.text: /impl.* handles it, because the longer regex is sorted ahead of /impl and matches the request first.
/impl handles it, because an exact string match always takes precedence over a regex match.
/impl handles it, because paths within a type are sorted in increasing order of string length.
Neither handles it, because ImplementationSpecific paths are treated as Prefix matches by Cilium.

questions.explanation: Cilium treats ImplementationSpecific as a regular expression and orders matches by decreasing string length within each path type. The regex /impl.* is longer than /impl, so it is sorted ahead, and because the * operator lets it match /impl as well, the shorter /impl match is never reached.

optionRationale.b: Exact is a separate path type with its own precedence; both of these paths are ImplementationSpecific, so no exact match is involved.
optionRationale.c: The sort is in decreasing order of string length, not increasing, so the longer regex comes first.
optionRationale.d: Cilium defines ImplementationSpecific to be Regex, not Prefix; the excerpt notes that some other implementations use Prefix.

questions.stem: A new pod is started in a Cilium-managed cluster. In what order does Cilium handle it?

options.text: It creates an endpoint from the orchestration system event, then resolves the endpoint's identity.
It resolves the identity first, then creates the endpoint from the orchestration system event.
It creates the endpoint and assigns an identity only once the pod receives traffic.
It resolves the identity from the orchestration system event without creating an endpoint.

questions.explanation: When a pod or workload is started, Cilium first creates an endpoint based on the event received from the orchestration system to represent it on the network. As a next step, Cilium resolves the identity of the endpoint created.

optionRationale.b: The order is reversed: the endpoint is created first, and the identity is resolved as a next step.
optionRationale.c: Identity resolution follows endpoint creation directly; it does not wait for traffic.
optionRationale.d: An endpoint is always created to represent the workload on the network.

A record of the security policies applied to a node.

optionRationale.c: Endpoints are created from orchestration system events, not manually by an administrator.

questions.stem: A client sends a GET request to the path /details on the gateway's external address. Which backend receives the request?

options.text: The details service on port 9080
The productpage service on port 9080
The my-gateway service on port 80
No backend, because the request lacks the magic header

questions.explanation: The HTTPRoute defines a rule that matches the path prefix /details and sends traffic to the details service on port 9080. The second rule, which targets productpage, requires the magic header, the great query parameter, the / path prefix and the GET method, so a plain GET /details does not match it.

optionRationale.b: productpage is the backend of the second rule, which also requires the magic header and the great query parameter.
optionRationale.c: my-gateway is the Gateway resource that listens on port 80; it is not a backend service.
optionRationale.d: The magic header is required only by the second rule; the first rule matches /details without it.

questions.stem: You want the Cilium Operator's Prometheus endpoint to require clients to present a certificate, verified against a CA. You already have a secret with tls.crt and tls.key. What must you add to that secret, and which Helm flag enables the verification?

options.text: Add ca.crt to the secret and set operator.prometheus.tls.server.mtls.enabled=true
Add ca.crt to the secret and set operator.prometheus.tls.enabled=true

questions.explanation: Mutual TLS on Operator Prometheus requires the ca.crt key in the same secret as tls.crt and tls.key, and the flag operator.prometheus.tls.server.mtls.enabled=true, which uses ca.crt to verify client certificates.

optionRationale.b: operator.prometheus.tls.enabled only turns on TLS; it does not enable verification of client certificates.
optionRationale.c: The required key is ca.crt, not tls.ca.
optionRationale.d: existingSecret takes the secret name; it is not a boolean that enables mTLS.

options.text: It uses ca.crt from the secret to verify client certificates.
It uses ca.crt from the secret to verify the operator's own serving certificate.
It generates a new CA and client certificates automatically.
It encrypts the secret at rest in the cluster.

questions.explanation: The mtls flag makes the Operator Prometheus endpoint use the ca.crt key of the secret to verify certificates presented by clients, which is what mutual TLS adds on top of plain TLS.

optionRationale.b: The CA verifies client certificates, not the operator's serving certificate.
optionRationale.c: The flag consumes an existing ca.crt in the secret; it does not generate certificates.
optionRationale.d: The flag concerns TLS client verification, not secret storage.

questions.stem: A team applies the Gateway and HTTPRoute below. Requests arriving at the Gateway on port 80 with the path /echo are sent to which backends, and in what proportion?

options.text: All requests go to echo-1 on port 8080, because the first backendRef in the list takes precedence.
Requests are split evenly, 50/50, between echo-1 on port 8080 and echo-2 on port 8090.
Requests are split 50/50 between echo-1 and echo-2, but both are contacted on port 8080.
Requests are rejected until the Gateway reports an address in its ADDRESS column.

questions.explanation: The HTTPRoute defines a single rule matching the path prefix /echo, with two backendRefs carrying weight 50 each. The weights are equal, so traffic is split evenly between the two Services, each on the port given in its own backendRef: echo-1 on 8080 and echo-2 on 8090.

optionRationale.a: Both backendRefs are listed with equal weights, so neither takes precedence; the split is even rather than first-match.
optionRationale.c: Each backendRef carries its own port, and the manifest gives echo-2 port 8090, not 8080.
optionRationale.d: The Gateway is created and listens on port 80; an empty ADDRESS column in the get output does not cause requests to be rejected.

apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Gateway
metadata:
  name: cilium-gw
spec:
  gatewayClassName: cilium
  listeners:
  - protocol: HTTP
    port: 80
    name: web-gw-echo
    allowedRoutes:
      namespaces:
        from: Same
---
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: HTTPRoute
metadata:
  name: example-route-1
spec:
  parentRefs:
  - name: cilium-gw
  rules:
  - matches:
    - path:
        type: PathPrefix
        value: /echo
    backendRefs:
    - kind: Service
      name: echo-1
      port: 8080
      weight: 50
    - kind: Service
      name: echo-2
      port: 8090
      weight: 50

questions.stem: A platform team wants every Cilium-managed endpoint in the cluster to be able to reach kube-dns on port 53/UDP, without listing each client workload. Which manifest achieves this?

options.text: A CiliumClusterwideNetworkPolicy whose endpointSelector matches the kube-dns pods and whose ingress rule uses an empty fromEndpoints entry with toPorts port "53" protocol UDP.
A CiliumNetworkPolicy in the kube-system namespace whose endpointSelector matches the kube-dns pods and whose egress rule uses an empty toEndpoints entry with toPorts port "53" protocol UDP.
A CiliumClusterwideNetworkPolicy whose endpointSelector matches all endpoints in the cluster and whose egress rule allows port "53" protocol UDP to any destination.
A CiliumNetworkPolicy in each application namespace whose endpointSelector matches the client pods and whose ingress rule allows port "53" protocol UDP.

questions.explanation: The example is a CiliumClusterwideNetworkPolicy that selects the kube-dns pods in kube-system and permits ingress to them from any endpoint, because the fromEndpoints list contains an empty selector. The port is restricted to 53/UDP.

optionRationale.b: The policy selects kube-dns and must describe traffic arriving at kube-dns, so the rule belongs under ingress, not egress; a namespaced policy also would not cover the whole cluster.
optionRationale.c: Selecting all endpoints and allowing egress to any destination is the opposite direction and does not restrict traffic to kube-dns on port 53/UDP.
optionRationale.d: A per-namespace policy selecting clients with an ingress rule does not match the kube-dns pods and does not scale to all Cilium-managed endpoints.

The empty fromEndpoints entry matches only endpoints in the same namespace as the selected pods, so pods outside kube-system are excluded.
The policy is cluster-wide, so it overrides any other policy and blocks all traffic that is not explicitly listed, including DNS from other kube-system pods.
The toPorts entry restricts traffic to UDP only, so any pod using TCP for DNS is denied.

questions.explanation: The endpointSelector uses matchLabels with the kube-system namespace and the k8s-app: kube-dns label, so the policy applies to the kube-dns endpoints. The empty fromEndpoints entry allows all Cilium-managed endpoints to reach those selected pods on 53/UDP; it does not grant or govern traffic to unrelated pods in kube-system.

optionRationale.c: Being cluster-wide changes the scope of the policy, not the direction of the rule; the rule is an ingress allow to the selected kube-dns pods.
optionRationale.d: The port entry does specify UDP, but the question concerns a pod that cannot reach kube-dns on 53/UDP, so the protocol is not the cause.

questions.stem: A team applies the Gateway and HTTPRoute below. Requests to /echo are sent to two Services, echo-1 on port 8080 and echo-2 on port 8090. How is traffic distributed between them?

options.text: Evenly, 50/50, because both backendRefs carry a weight of 50.
All traffic goes to echo-1, because it is listed first and weights are ignored for Services.
All traffic goes to echo-2, because port 8090 is not the listener port of 80.
Traffic is split by path prefix, with /echo going to echo-1 and any other path to echo-2.

questions.explanation: The HTTPRoute lists two backendRefs, echo-1 on port 8080 and echo-2 on port 8090, each with weight 50. The weights are equal, so the split between the two Services is even at 50/50.

optionRationale.b: The order of backendRefs does not determine routing here; the weights of 50 and 50 produce an even split rather than sending everything to the first Service.
optionRationale.c: The backend Service ports (8080 and 8090) are independent of the Gateway listener port of 80, and echo-2 receives its weighted share of traffic.
optionRationale.d: The route has a single match on the /echo path prefix with both Services as backends; it does not route different paths to different Services.

attachments.title: The Gateway and HTTPRoute under test
attachments.body:
---
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Gateway
metadata:
  name: cilium-gw
spec:
  gatewayClassName: cilium
  listeners:
  - protocol: HTTP
    port: 80
    name: web-gw-echo
    allowedRoutes:
      namespaces:
        from: Same
---
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: HTTPRoute
metadata:
  name: example-route-1
spec:
  parentRefs:
  - name: cilium-gw
  rules:
  - matches:
    - path:
        type: PathPrefix
        value: /echo
    backendRefs:
    - kind: Service
      name: echo-1
      port: 8080
      weight: 50
    - kind: Service
      name: echo-2
      port: 8090
      weight: 50

The request is denied, because the policy only allows pods under the "leia" service account to initiate connections.
The request is allowed, but only if the destination pod also runs under the "luke" service account.

questions.explanation: The policy selects destination pods labelled with the "leia" service account and allows ingress from endpoints labelled with the "luke" service account, on TCP port 80, with an HTTP rule permitting GET on the /public path. A request matching all of these is allowed.

optionRationale.b: The policy specifies protocol: TCP for port 80, not UDP.
optionRationale.c: "leia" is the destination selected by endpointSelector; the allowed source is "luke".
optionRationale.d: The destination must match the endpointSelector label "leia"; "luke" is the source label.

attachments.title: The policy under test
attachments.body:
apiVersion: "cilium.io/v2"
kind: CiliumNetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: "k8s-svc-account"
spec:
  endpointSelector:
    matchLabels:
      io.cilium.k8s.policy.serviceaccount: leia
  ingress:
  - fromEndpoints:
    - matchLabels:
        io.cilium.k8s.policy.serviceaccount: luke
    toPorts:
    - ports:
      - port: '80'
        protocol: TCP
      rules:
        http:
        - method: GET
          path: "/public$"

citations.title: Example
citations.quote:
The following example grants any pod running under the service account of
"luke" to issue a ``HTTP GET /public`` request on TCP port 80 to all pods
running associated to the service account of "leia".

questions.stem: A platform team applies a CiliumNetworkPolicy directly with kubectl into the namespace `payments`. The policy's endpointSelector matches `app=ledger` and its rule contains no namespace selector. Which pods does the rule apply to?

options.text: Only pods labelled `app=ledger` in the `payments` namespace.
Pods labelled `app=ledger` in every namespace of the cluster.
All pods in the `payments` namespace, regardless of their labels.
No pods, because a namespace selector is mandatory for imported policies.

questions.explanation: Policies imported directly with the API apply to all namespaces unless a namespace selector is specified. The absence of a namespace selector therefore widens the rule to matching pods cluster-wide, not just the namespace the object was created in.

optionRationale.a: This assumes the creating namespace confines the rule, but the policy applies to all namespaces unless a namespace selector is specified.
optionRationale.c: The endpointSelector still restricts the rule to pods labelled `app=ledger`; the namespace selector is what is missing, not the label selector.
optionRationale.d: A namespace selector is optional; without one the policy simply applies to all namespaces.

citations.title: Using Kubernetes Constructs In Policy
citations.quote:
Network policies imported directly with the api_ref apply to all
namespaces unless a namespace selector is specified as described in
example_cnp_ns_boundaries.

questions.stem: A platform team applies the two policies below, one in ns1 and one in ns2. A pod in ns1 then sends traffic to a pod in ns2. What is the result?

options.text: The traffic is allowed, because the empty matchLabels selector matches every endpoint in the cluster.
The traffic is dropped, because the destination pod in ns2 only accepts traffic from endpoints in ns2.
The traffic is allowed, because the policy in ns1 has no egress section and therefore does not restrict egress.
The traffic is dropped, because the policy in ns1 has no egress section and therefore denies all egress by default.

questions.explanation: Each policy selects all pods in its own namespace and allows ingress only from endpoints carrying the same (empty) label set, which in practice means endpoints in the same namespace. The destination pod in ns2 is therefore not permitted to receive traffic from a pod in ns1, so the connection is dropped. Note that the ns1 policy does not restrict egress at all, so the drop is enforced at the destination side.

optionRationale.a: The empty selector is evaluated within the policy's namespace context, not cluster-wide; the excerpt states that both source and destination have to be in the same namespace.
optionRationale.c: It is true that the ns1 policy does not restrict egress, but that does not make the connection succeed, because the ns2 policy still blocks ingress from ns1.
optionRationale.d: A policy with no egress section does not deny egress; the excerpt says pods can still communicate egress to anywhere unless the destination is in ns1 or ns2.

attachments.title: The policies applied in ns1 and ns2
attachments.body:
apiVersion: "cilium.io/v2"
kind: CiliumNetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: "isolate-ns1"
  namespace: ns1
spec:
  endpointSelector:
    matchLabels:
      {}
  ingress:
  - fromEndpoints:
    - matchLabels:
        {}
---
apiVersion: "cilium.io/v2"
kind: CiliumNetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: "isolate-ns1"
  namespace: ns2
spec:
  endpointSelector:
    matchLabels:
      {}
  ingress:
  - fromEndpoints:
    - matchLabels:
        {}

citations.title: Example
citations.quote:
This means that the pods can still communicate egress to anywhere
	  unless the destination is in either ``ns1`` or ``ns2`` in which case
	  both source and destination have to be in the same namespace.
